question: A new service desk analyst at a 3,000-store retail chain notices three AI things in ServiceNow: a 'Summarize' option on incidents, a chat assistant employees use on the portal, and a manager talking about 'AI agents that triage tickets'. She asks you: 'Aren't these all the same chatbot?' Explain the difference between a Now Assist skill, a conversational assistant (Virtual Agent / ServiceNow Otto), and an AI agent, and why a human still reviews the output.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That you can separate the layers of ServiceNow AI instead of calling everything a chatbot: a single-purpose generative skill, a conversational front door, and goal-driven agents that plan and use tools. Bonus points for knowing that in 2026 ServiceNow put these behind one brand, ServiceNow Otto, while the building blocks (skills, AI Agent Studio) still exist underneath.

The Answer

1. A Now Assist skill is one generative AI task wired into a specific place. 'Summarize' on an incident reads the record (description, work notes, comments) and asks an LLM to produce a summary. It does one job, on demand, for the person looking at the record. Other examples: resolution notes generation, knowledge article drafting from a resolved case. An admin turns skills on per workflow in the Now Assist Admin console.

2. The conversational assistant is the chat experience employees use on the portal or in Teams/Slack. Classic Virtual Agent ran scripted topics; newer versions use an LLM to understand the request and pick the right topic, search knowledge, or start a catalog request. ServiceNow announced Otto in May 2026 as the single front door that unifies Now Assist, Moveworks and the AI experience, so in newer instances the portal assistant may be branded Otto. The ServiceNow developer blog is explicit that Otto is the user-facing assistant and routes work to agents; it is not the agents themselves.

3. An AI agent is given an objective rather than a single task, for example 'triage this incident'. It reasons about the steps, calls tools (look up similar incidents, check the CI, set the assignment group) and can work with other agents in an agentic workflow. These are built and managed in AI Agent Studio. Agents can run supervised (a person approves their actions) or autonomous.

A simple analogy for the analyst: a skill is a calculator button, the assistant is the receptionist, and an agent is a junior colleague you hand a task to.

Why a human still reviews: LLM output is probabilistic. ServiceNow's own docs warn that generated output can be inaccurate or incomplete and recommend human oversight. A summary can miss the one work note that matters; an agent can pick the wrong group. So analysts check summaries before sending them to a customer, and high-impact agent actions start in supervised mode.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling every AI feature 'Virtual Agent'.
  • Assuming agents replace ACLs. They act within the platform's security model, so access controls still apply.
  • Thinking the rebrand changed what is configured. Existing agents still live in AI Agent Studio.
Score points: Mention that Otto is the front door and agents are what it routes to, and that supervised mode is the normal way to start with agents.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Where would you switch a skill on or off for only the IT service desk?
  • What is the difference between supervised and autonomous execution of an AI agent?
  • How would you stop the assistant from answering questions about salaries?

Sources

  • Otto vs Now Assist: what actually changed (ServiceNow Developer Advocate blog)
  • AI Agent Studio (ServiceNow docs)
  • Use an AI agent action (ServiceNow docs, Workflow Studio)

question: A mid-size auto-parts manufacturer is moving its first automation to Workflow Studio: 'When a quality defect record is raised on a production line, notify the line supervisor, create a task for the quality engineer, and if the defect is critical, ask the plant manager for approval to stop the line.' A junior admin asks you what a flow, a subflow, an action and a trigger are, and which of them they need here. Explain.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Clear definitions of the four building blocks, and a sensible split of this process into them. Interviewers also listen for reuse thinking: what would another plant or team want to call again?

The Answer

  • Trigger: what starts a flow. Types include record triggers (created, updated, created or updated), scheduled triggers, application triggers such as Service Catalog, and inbound email. Here: a record created trigger on the defect table.
  • Flow: the business process with exactly one trigger and a sequence of actions and flow logic (If, For Each, Wait for condition, Make a decision). Here: the 'Quality defect raised' flow.
  • Subflow: a reusable sequence with inputs and outputs and no trigger. Another flow, a script, or an AI agent can call it. Here: 'Request line stop approval' is a good subflow, because the maintenance process will probably need the same logic.
  • Action: a single reusable step, such as Create Record, Send Email, Ask for Approval, or a spoke action that calls an external system. Custom actions are built in the Action Designer with steps (script, REST, lookup) and are the right home for code.

A design for this request:

  1. Trigger: Created on the defect table (condition: active).
  2. Action: Send Notification to the line supervisor (use a notification record rather than a hard-coded email, so wording can change without editing the flow).
  3. Action: Create Task for the quality engineer, linked to the defect.
  4. Flow logic: If severity is Critical, call the subflow 'Request line stop approval' (input: defect record; output: approved yes/no).
  5. Inside the subflow: Ask for Approval from the plant manager with a due date; return the result. The parent flow updates the defect with the decision.

ServiceNow's flow guidelines say to use subflows for reusable logic and for flows that grow beyond roughly 25 actions, and to use a subflow (not a flow with an unneeded trigger) when a script needs to start the logic.

Common Mistakes

  • Building three separate flows on the same table with overlapping trigger conditions. They can conflict; give each flow unique conditions.
  • Starting the flow on every update and then using Wait for condition to filter. Prefer a record trigger with a condition.
  • Putting long scripts inline in the flow instead of in a custom action or Script Include.
  • Expecting a record trigger to fire when data is loaded by an update set or XML import. It does not.
Score points: Say which piece you would make reusable and why. Mention that Service Catalog tables use the Service Catalog trigger, not a record trigger.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you test this flow before activating it?
  • Where do you look when the flow did not run for a defect?
  • The approval rules differ per plant. How would you avoid hard-coding them?

Sources

  • General guidelines for Workflow Studio flows, subflows, and actions (ServiceNow docs)
  • Make a decision flow logic (ServiceNow docs)

question: A regional hospital has just switched on its CMDB. A new junior admin looks at the class list and asks: "Why do we have separate classes for Linux Server, Windows Server and Database Instance? Why can't we put every device in one cmdb_ci table with a 'type' field?" Explain what a CI class is and why ServiceNow models the CMDB as a class hierarchy.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That you understand a CI class is a table in an extension hierarchy rooted at cmdb_ci, that child classes inherit fields and add their own, and that class choice drives identification, health checks, relationships and what downstream processes (Incident, Change, Event Management) can do with the record. A flat table with a "type" string throws all of that away.

The Answer

A CI class is a table that represents one kind of configuration item. Every class extends cmdb_ci, directly or through intermediate classes. For example, cmdb_ci_linux_server extends cmdb_ci_server, which extends cmdb_ci_computer, which extends cmdb_ci_hardware, which extends cmdb_ci. A Linux server record therefore has the generic fields (name, owned by, support group, operational status) plus the hardware fields (serial number, manufacturer), plus server and Linux-specific fields.

The hierarchy matters for four practical reasons:

  • Identification. The Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE) uses identification rules defined per class. A server is matched on serial number or name; a database instance is a dependent CI and is identified through the host it runs on. A single flat table cannot express "this kind of thing is unique only in the context of its parent".
  • Right fields for the right thing. A hospital's infusion-pump gateway does not need a "number of CPUs" field, and a server does not need a "clinical location" field. Class-specific fields keep forms clean and data meaningful.
  • Health and governance. CMDB Health completeness (required and recommended fields), staleness and orphan rules are configured per class, so you can say "every Windows server must have a support group" without forcing that on printers.
  • Querying. Because child classes extend parents, a query on cmdb_ci_server returns Linux, Windows and AIX servers together, while a query on cmdb_ci_linux_server returns only Linux. You get both broad and narrow views from the same data.

Where to see it: CI Class Manager shows the tree, each class's fields, identification rule, reconciliation rules and health settings in one place.

Common Mistakes

  • Creating a custom class for every local nuance (for example a separate class per hospital site). Location is an attribute, not a class.
  • Storing servers in the base cmdb_ci table, which leaves them without a meaningful identification rule and invisible to class-based reports.
  • Extending an out-of-box class without checking whether an existing class already fits; custom classes need their own identification rule or IRE cannot match them.
Score points: Mention that a database instance or a network adapter is a dependent CI identified via its relationship to a host, which is something a flat table design simply cannot represent.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you decide whether to create a custom CI class or reuse an existing one?
  • What is the difference between an independent and a dependent identification rule?
  • Where in the platform would you look to see which fields a class inherits?

Sources

  • Components and process of Identification and Reconciliation - ServiceNow Docs
  • CMDB Health KPIs and metrics - ServiceNow Docs

question: A university IT team is starting with CSDM. In a workshop the registrar's office says: "Our Student Records system is one thing. Why does IT keep talking about a business application, a production instance, a business service and an offering for it?" Explain the difference between these records using the Student Records example.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That you can separate the portfolio view (what software we own), the operational view (the running deployment), and the consumer view (what people actually use and get support for), and that you know the tables. Knowing that CSDM 5 relabelled some of these is a plus.

The Answer

CSDM splits one "system" into records that answer different questions:

  • Business application (cmdb_ci_business_app): "Student Records" as a product in the application portfolio. Owner, vendor, lifecycle, cost, architecture type. It is not something that can break at 2 a.m.; it is the portfolio entry. It lives in the Design & Planning part of CSDM.
  • Service instance (cmdb_ci_service_auto and its subclasses; labelled "application service" before CSDM 5): the running deployment, for example "Student Records - Production" and "Student Records - Test". This is what is linked to the servers, databases and load balancers, ideally via Service Mapping or a dynamic CI group. Incidents and changes are raised against it. It belongs to the Service Delivery domain.
  • Business service (cmdb_ci_service_business): how the university presents it to its consumers, for example "Student Administration Services". It sits in the Service Consumption domain and is what users see in the portal.
  • Service offering (service_offering): the specific, supportable variant, for example "Student Records - Staff access" and "Student Records - Student self-service", each with its own commitments, support group and approval group.

The chain is: offering belongs to a business service; the offering depends on the service instance; the service instance is linked back to the business application it is a deployment of. That chain lets a single incident on a failing database server show which student-facing offering is impacted and who owns the product.

Why bother

  • Users pick "Student self-service" in the portal and do not need to know server names.
  • Incident routing and change approval come from the offering and service instance, not from someone's memory.
  • Portfolio decisions (retire, replace) are made on the business application without disturbing operational records.

Common Mistakes

  • Putting servers directly under the business application. The business application is not an operational CI; infrastructure relates to the service instance.
  • Creating one record per environment of the business application instead of one business application with several service instances.
  • Using the old generic cmdb_ci_service table for everything.
Score points: Note that CSDM 5 renamed labels (application service to service instance, technical service to technology management service) without renaming the underlying tables, so existing reports and integrations keep working.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Where would a technology management service such as 'Database Hosting' fit in this picture?
  • How do you link infrastructure CIs to a service instance without Service Mapping?
  • Which CSDM record should an incident's Service and Service offering fields point to?

Sources

  • CSDM data domains - ServiceNow Docs
  • Top features of CSDM 5 - ServiceNow Community
  • Service Delivery domain in the CSDM model - ServiceNow Docs

question: A telecom operator sells mobile plans to 2 million households and also sells fibre and SD-WAN to 3,000 businesses. Their contact-centre manager is new to ServiceNow and asks: "Why does the consultant keep talking about accounts, contacts and consumers? Aren't they all just customers?" Explain the difference and how each side of the business would be modelled in Customer Service Management.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A clear explanation of the B2B and B2C models in CSM and the core tables behind them, linked to how the telco actually sells. Bonus for knowing that one instance can run both models side by side.

The Answer

CSM supports two primary business models, and the telco has both.

B2B: the 3,000 business customers.

  • An account is the company that buys the service. Accounts live in the Account table [customer_account], which extends the Company table. Accounts can be customers, partners, or both, and can be arranged in hierarchies, such as a retail chain with regional subsidiaries.
  • A contact is a person who works for that account, for example the customer's IT manager who reports an SD-WAN outage. Contacts live in [customer_contact], which extends the User table, and each contact belongs to one account.
  • Cases are logged against the account and contact. Visibility is then shared across the account: a customer admin contact can see all of the company's cases, not just their own.

B2C: the 2 million households.

  • A consumer is an individual customer, stored in [csm_consumer]. There is no company in between.
  • A household [csm_household] groups consumers at the same address who share products, such as a family plan. The head of household can see the other members' cases.

Why it matters for the contact centre:

  • Agents see different context. A B2B agent sees the account, its contracts, assets and other open cases. A B2C agent sees the person and their household.
  • Entitlements and SLAs differ. Businesses usually have contract-based response times. Consumers usually get standard service levels.
  • Portals differ. The B2B portal works around account access and contacts. Consumer self-service is built around an individual login.

So yes, they are all customers, but the platform stores them differently because the relationship is different.

Common Mistakes

  • Creating every household as an account, which makes millions of fake companies and breaks reporting.
  • Storing business contacts as plain users with no account link, which loses account-level visibility.
  • Thinking you need two instances for B2B and B2C.
Score points: Ask early about sole traders and small businesses. Whether a one-person business is an account or a consumer is a classic design decision you should settle before data migration.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you model a business customer whose employees also have personal mobile plans?
  • What does a customer admin contact see that a normal contact does not?
  • Where do products and assets fit into this model?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: Customer data
  • ServiceNow Docs: Roles installed with Customer Service Management
  • ServiceNow Community: Consumer vs customer, which portal?

question: A 6,000-employee hospital network has just gone live on HR Service Delivery. A nurse submits two requests in Employee Center on the same day: one about a missing night-shift differential on her payslip, and one about adding her newborn to her medical plan. She notices the requests went to different HR teams with different case numbers and asks the service desk why HR "split her up". Explain, in plain terms, what an HR case, a Center of Excellence (COE) and an HR service are, and why her two requests were routed differently.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That you understand the basic HRSD data model: every HR request becomes an HR case, cases are organised by Center of Excellence, and the HR service the employee picks decides which COE, template and team handle it. A good answer explains this in language an employee or HR business partner would follow.

The Answer

HR case. Every HR request is stored as a case. The base table is HR Case [sn_hr_core_case]. It holds the subject person (the nurse), the opened-for person, the HR service, state, assignment group and SLA.

Center of Excellence (COE). A COE is a specialist HR function such as Payroll, Benefits, Talent Management or Workforce Administration. In the platform, each COE is a table that extends the HR case table, for example sn_hr_core_case_payroll and sn_hr_core_case_benefits. Because they are separate child tables, each one can have its own fields, forms, assignment rules and security.

HR service. An HR service is the specific thing an employee asks for, such as "Payroll discrepancy" or "Add a dependent to benefits". The service record points to a COE, a topic category and topic detail, an HR case template that pre-fills fields, and optionally a record producer so it appears in Employee Center.

Why she got two cases.

  1. The payslip question used a payroll service, so the case was created in the Payroll COE table and assigned to the payroll team.
  2. The newborn request used a benefits service, so it landed in the Benefits COE with a different template, SLA and team. It may also need documents such as a birth certificate.
  3. Splitting them is intentional. Payroll staff should not see her medical dependants, and benefits staff do not need her pay details. COE-level security keeps that separation.

For the nurse, the experience is still one place. Both cases show under My Requests in Employee Center, and she can follow each one there.

Common Mistakes

  • Describing HR cases as incidents with a different label. HR cases have their own scoped app, roles and security model.
  • Suggesting one generic case for everything. That breaks COE security and reporting by function.
  • Confusing the HR service (what is requested) with the record producer (the form the employee fills in).
Score points: Mention that topic category and topic detail sit under each COE and drive reporting, and that HR services should be set up only after that taxonomy is agreed with HR.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Where would you look to see which HR case template a service uses?
  • If HR wants one case to have tasks for both payroll and benefits, how could you model that?
  • How does the employee see case progress without seeing internal work notes?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: Configure an HR service
  • ServiceNow Docs: HR COE security policies
  • ServiceNow Docs: HR service administration

question: At a regional bank, the IT platform team owns ServiceNow and every engineer on it holds the admin role. After HR Service Delivery goes live, the HR director asks: "Can your admins read our grievance and salary cases?" One of the engineers says, "Admin sees everything, so yes." Is that correct, and how does HRSD protect sensitive HR data from system administrators?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That HRSD deliberately limits what platform admins see, that HR access is driven by HR-specific roles, and that there is a recommended step after setup to stop admins inheriting HR administration. The candidate should also show they know admin can still do things like elevate roles, so process and auditing matter too.

The Answer

The engineer is mostly wrong. HRSD is a scoped application with its own ACLs, and the documented design is that a system administrator has limited visibility into HR data:

  • Admins cannot create HR profiles, see only limited profile and case data, and cannot see comments or work notes.
  • On HR cases and tasks, attachments, work notes, comments, description and payload are restricted to authorised HR staff.
  • Personal information on HR profiles is hidden from system administrators.

Access is granted through HR roles:

  • sn_hr_core.case_reader and sn_hr_core.case_writer to read or work HR cases and tasks.
  • sn_hr_core.profile_reader and sn_hr_core.profile_writer for HR profile data.
  • sn_hr_core.secure_info_reader as an example role for more sensitive profile and case data.
  • sn_hr_core.admin, the HR administrator, who can do everything and see all HR data.

The key step: during implementation the HR admin role is often contained in admin so the build team can configure. ServiceNow's guidance is to remove sn_hr_core.admin from the admin role after setup so IT admins cannot browse HR records. There is also an HR property, "If true, ACLs check if the user is being impersonated", under HR Administration > Properties. Set to true, it stops HR data showing when someone impersonates an HR user.

COE security policies then narrow access further, so for example only Employee Relations groups see ER cases.

Be honest with the HR director about the limits. An admin can still grant themselves roles. Govern that with role-change auditing, alerts on HR role assignment, and a break-glass process.

Common Mistakes

  • Leaving sn_hr_core.admin inside admin after go-live.
  • Testing HR security by impersonating with the impersonation check property switched off.
  • Claiming HR data is fully invisible to admins. It is restricted, not physically isolated.
Score points: Suggest a scheduled report or alert on sys_user_has_role changes for HR roles, so the HR director gets evidence, not just a promise.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you give a service-desk agent read access to only one COE?
  • What does the impersonation property change during UAT?
  • Where would you look if an HR agent says they cannot see a case assigned to their group?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: HR profile and HR case security
  • ServiceNow Docs: HR COE security policies

question: A national retailer has 600 stores, each with a small server rack and a point-of-sale network behind a firewall. The ServiceNow instance is in the cloud. A store operations manager asks: "How can ServiceNow possibly find what's inside our stores if it can't see our network?" Explain what a MID Server is and how Discovery uses it.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That the instance never reaches into the customer network directly; a MID Server inside the network does the work and talks outbound to the instance. Bonus points for describing the Discovery phases at a high level and the basics of where MID Servers should sit.

The Answer

A MID Server (Management, Instrumentation and Discovery) is a Java application that runs as a Windows service or a Linux daemon on a server inside the customer's network. It connects outbound over HTTPS to the instance and polls the ECC Queue for work. Because the connection is outbound, the retailer does not need to open inbound firewall ports from the internet into its stores.

How Discovery uses it:

  1. A Discovery schedule on the instance says what to scan (IP ranges, for example each store's subnet) and when.
  2. The instance writes probe requests to the ECC Queue; the chosen MID Server picks them up.
  3. Scanning: the MID Server runs the Shazzam probe and port probes to find live hosts and which ports answer (SSH, WMI, SNMP and so on).
  4. Classification: based on the ports, it sends one classification probe to work out what the device is, for example a Windows server versus a network switch.
  5. Identification and exploration: a pattern (or legacy probes and sensors) logs in with stored credentials and collects details such as OS version, installed software, running processes and network connections.
  6. Results go back through the ECC Queue and are written to the CMDB through the Identification and Reconciliation Engine, so an existing CI is updated instead of duplicated.

For 600 stores, you would not install a MID Server in every store. Typically MID Servers sit in regional data centres or hubs that have network reach to the store subnets, each assigned the IP ranges it can reach, with more than one per region so that one failing does not stop discovery.

Common Mistakes

  • Saying the instance "scans the network directly". It cannot; everything goes through a MID Server.
  • Forgetting credentials. Without valid SSH/WMI/SNMP credentials, Discovery only gets as far as classification and you end up with thin CIs.
  • Installing one MID Server and pointing it at everything; it becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck.
Score points: Mention that MID Server selection can be driven by assigned applications, IP ranges and capabilities, so store subnets automatically route to the MID Servers that can actually reach them.

Likely Follow-ups

  • What happens to Discovery if the MID Server goes down mid-schedule?
  • What credentials would you need to discover Windows servers versus network switches?
  • What is the ECC Queue and how would you use it to troubleshoot?

Sources

  • Horizontal discovery process flow with patterns - ServiceNow Docs
  • MID Server selection - ServiceNow Docs
  • ServiceNow ITOM interview questions thread - ServiceNow Community

question: A 600-bed hospital has just gone live on Incident Management. On day one, a ward clerk reports that the printer at a nurses' station is jammed, and ten minutes later the radiology team reports that the image viewing system is down for every reading room. A new service desk agent asks why they cannot simply type "1 - Critical" into the Priority field for the radiology call. Explain how ServiceNow decides incident priority, why the field behaves this way, and how the priority affects what happens next.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That priority is derived, not typed: it comes from Impact and Urgency through priority lookup rules. They also want to hear why that matters (consistency, SLAs and escalations hang off it) and who is allowed to change the mapping.

The Answer

On the base Incident form the Priority field is read-only. Agents set two inputs:

  • Impact: how widely the business is affected (1 - High, 2 - Medium, 3 - Low). One nurses' station printer is low; every reading room in radiology is high.
  • Urgency: how fast the business needs a fix (1 - High, 2 - Medium, 3 - Low). Radiology cannot read scans for the emergency department, so urgency is high.

A data lookup table, the Priority Lookup Rules (All > System Policy > Rules > Priority Lookup Rules), maps each Impact/Urgency pair to a Priority. In the base data, 1/1 gives 1 - Critical, 2/2 gives 3 - Moderate and 3/3 gives 5 - Planning. So the radiology outage becomes P1 and the jammed printer becomes something like P4 or P5, whichever agent logs them.

Why it is built this way:

  • Consistency. If every agent picked their own priority, a busy shift would label everything P1 and the label would mean nothing.
  • Downstream automation. SLA definitions usually key off priority (for example, a P1 response target of 15 minutes). So do notifications to on-call staff, escalation rules, and major incident trigger criteria. A wrong priority starts the wrong clock and pages the wrong people.
  • Governance. Only administrators and data lookup administrators can edit the lookup rules. The matrix is agreed with the business once and is not argued on every ticket.

What happens next for the radiology P1: the P1 SLA attaches, the assignment group is notified, and if the hospital uses Major Incident Management, the incident may be proposed as a major incident. The printer ticket just joins the queue.

If the hospital wants a different matrix, for example where any incident on a clinical system never drops below P2, the right move is to change the lookup rules or add a condition-based rule. Removing the read-only behaviour so agents can pick freely is the wrong move.

Common Mistakes

  • Saying the agent should just edit Priority, or advising a client script that unlocks the field.
  • Mixing up impact (breadth) with urgency (time sensitivity).
  • Forgetting that changing the matrix changes SLA attachment on new records, which affects reporting.
Score points: Mention that priority lookup rules are a data lookup (a no-code, table-driven rule). Then point out that changing Impact or Urgency later recalculates Priority, which can reset or attach a different SLA, depending on how the SLA definitions are built.

Likely Follow-ups

  • The hospital wants clinical systems to be at least P2 regardless of impact. How would you do it without code?
  • What happens to an in-progress SLA when an agent lowers the urgency of a P1?
  • Where else in the platform are data lookup rules useful?

Sources

  • Define priority lookup rules (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Managing incident priority (ServiceNow Community ITSM blog)

question: A regional telco promises business broadband customers that faults will be fixed within 8 business hours. Internally, the field engineering team has agreed to reach a fault site within 4 hours, and a fibre wholesaler that supplies the last mile has a contract to repair its part within 6 hours. A junior analyst asks what the difference is between an SLA, an OLA and an underpinning contract, and how ServiceNow knows when to start and stop the clock. Explain both.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Clear definitions of the three agreement types, and the fact that ServiceNow models all three the same way: an SLA definition with conditions, a duration and a schedule. Each one creates a task SLA record on the ticket.

The Answer

The three agreement types:

  • SLA (Service Level Agreement): between the provider and the customer. Here, the 8-business-hour fix promised to broadband customers.
  • OLA (Operational Level Agreement): between internal teams of the provider. Here, field engineering's 4-hour arrival target, which supports the SLA.
  • Underpinning contract (UC): between the provider and an external supplier. Here, the wholesaler's 6-hour repair commitment.

The OLA and UC must be tighter than the SLA they support. Otherwise the telco can breach its customer promise even when every team meets its own target.

How ServiceNow models them: all three are SLA definition records (Service Level Management). The Type field says whether a definition is an SLA, OLA or underpinning contract. Each definition specifies:

  • Table: incident, or another task table.
  • Duration: for example 8 hours.
  • Schedule: for example business hours Monday to Friday 08:00 to 18:00. The schedule can come from the definition or from a field on the task, or there can be no schedule (24x7). A timezone source decides whose clock is used, such as the caller's, the definition's, or the location's.
  • Conditions:
    • Start: when the SLA attaches, for example Category is Broadband and Priority is 1 or 2.
    • Pause: stops the clock, for example State is On Hold with reason Awaiting Customer. The clock resumes when the condition stops matching.
    • Stop: completes the SLA, for example State is Resolved.
    • Reset: completes the current SLA and starts a fresh one if start conditions match again.
    • Cancel: cancels it, for example when start conditions stop matching, depending on configuration.

When start conditions match, the engine creates a task SLA (task_sla) record linked to the incident. It tracks elapsed time, business elapsed time, percentage, and whether the SLA has breached. That record drives the SLA timer on the form, breach notifications and reporting.

For the wholesaler UC, a common pattern is to start the clock when the incident is handed to the supplier (for example, an assignment group of "Wholesale Fibre") and stop it when it comes back.

Common Mistakes

  • Thinking OLAs and UCs need a different module. They are the same definition with a different Type.
  • Using 24x7 when the promise is in business hours.
  • Leaving out a pause condition, so the telco is penalised while waiting on the customer.
Score points: Mention retroactive start, which starts the clock from a task date field such as Created when an SLA attaches late, for example after a priority change. Also say that the SLA timeline on a task SLA shows exactly when the clock ran and paused.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Priority changes from P3 to P1 after two hours. What should happen to the SLA?
  • How would you report OLA performance per engineering team?
  • Where would you send a warning at 75% of the SLA?

question: A regional hospital network runs ServiceNow in the cloud, but its Active Directory domain controllers, a SQL Server patient-scheduling database and 4,000 servers sit inside a locked-down data centre. Security will not open any inbound firewall ports from the internet. A new admin asks: how can ServiceNow possibly reach those systems? What is a MID Server, and why does it solve this problem?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That you know the MID Server is the bridge between a cloud instance and systems behind a customer firewall, that the connection direction is outbound from the MID Server to the instance, and that it works through the ECC Queue rather than the instance calling into the network.

The Answer

A MID Server (Management, Instrumentation and Discovery) is a Java application the hospital installs on a Windows or Linux host inside its own network. It is registered to the instance with a dedicated user that holds the mid_server role.

  • Direction of traffic: the MID Server opens an outbound HTTPS connection to the instance (normally port 443) and polls for work. The instance never initiates a connection into the data centre, so the security team does not need to open inbound ports.
  • ECC Queue: the instance writes a job as an output record in the ECC Queue (ecc_queue). The MID Server picks it up, runs it locally (an LDAP query, a JDBC call, a PowerShell or SSH command, a Discovery probe) and posts the result back as an input record, which a sensor or flow then processes.
  • Typical uses at this hospital: LDAP user and group import from Active Directory, a JDBC data source reading the scheduling database into an import set, Discovery and Service Mapping of the 4,000 servers into the CMDB, and IntegrationHub actions that must call internal-only APIs.
  • Credentials are stored on the instance in the Credentials table (or an external vault) and used by the MID Server at run time, so passwords are not hard-coded in scripts.

In practice you deploy at least two MID Servers and put them in a cluster (load balance or failover) so that patching one host does not stop the LDAP import or Discovery schedule.

Common Mistakes

  • Saying the instance "connects to the MID Server". It is the other way round.
  • Installing one MID Server on a developer's laptop or on a domain controller. Use a dedicated, monitored server.
  • Forgetting that the MID Server must be validated after install and upgraded with the instance (it auto-upgrades to match the instance version).
  • Routing public SaaS calls through a MID Server when the instance can call the SaaS endpoint directly.
Score points: Mention that you check MID Server health from the MID Server record (status Up, validated) and that a backlog of ready output records in the ECC Queue is the first sign a MID Server is down or overloaded.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you size and cluster MID Servers for Discovery of 4,000 servers?
  • What happens to queued jobs if the only MID Server goes down for an hour?
  • When would you call an internal API through a MID Server instead of directly from the instance?

Sources

  • MID Server ECC Queue (ServiceNow docs)
  • The ECC queue for Discovery (ServiceNow docs)
  • Some questions about VPN and MID server (ServiceNow Community)

question: A university IT service desk says the 'All open incidents' list sometimes takes 15 seconds to load, but only when it is filtered on a custom field u_campus and sorted by that field. A junior admin wants to start adding indexes to every column. Before anyone touches the database, where in ServiceNow would you look to confirm the slow query, and what is an index and when does it actually help?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That you measure before you change anything, know the built-in diagnostics (transaction logs and the slow query log), understand what an index is in plain terms, and know that indexes are added deliberately, not to every column.

The Answer

Step 1: confirm where the time goes.

  • Transaction logs (System Logs > Transactions) show each request's total response time, broken into SQL time, business rule time, client network time and so on. If SQL time is most of the 15 seconds, the database query is the problem; if browser time dominates, it is a UI or client script problem instead.
  • Slow Queries (System Diagnostics > Stats > Slow Queries) groups similar slow SQL statements together with how often they ran and their average and total execution time. You should see a query pattern on incident with u_campus in the WHERE and ORDER BY clauses.
  • On a sub-production copy, Debug SQL (session debug) lets you watch the SQL a list generates.

Step 2: understand indexes. An index is like the index at the back of a textbook: a sorted structure that lets the database jump to matching rows instead of reading the entire table. If the incident table has two million rows and the list filters on a field with no index, the database may scan far more rows than needed and sort them in memory.

When an index helps: fields that appear repeatedly in filters, joins or sorts on large tables, where the value narrows the result set. When it does not: small tables, fields with very few distinct values used alone, or queries that start with a wildcard such as contains. Every index also slows down inserts and updates a little and uses storage.

Step 3: use the platform tool. From the slow query record an admin can use Suggest Index (the Index Suggestion Engine). Suggestions are reviewed under System Diagnostics > Index Suggestions and can be scheduled for a quiet time; index creation on big tables can run for an hour or more. If you are unsure, raise a case with ServiceNow Support rather than guessing.

Common Mistakes

  • Indexing every column "just in case".
  • Skipping the measurement step and blaming the database when a slow client script is the real cause.
  • Creating an index on a large table in the middle of the working day.
Score points: Say you would also check whether users even need the default "all open" list: a filter that limits rows, plus fewer columns, often fixes the problem without any index.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Why is a "contains" filter slow even when an index exists?
  • How would you prove the new index helped?
  • What is a composite index and why does column order matter?

Sources

  • Resolving slow queries (ServiceNow docs)
  • Generate an index suggestion for a slow query (ServiceNow docs)
  • Schedule a slow-query index suggestion for creation (ServiceNow docs)

question: A national retailer's test instance is eight months out of date, so testers keep finding bugs that do not exist in production. The release manager asks you to clone production over test before the holiday code freeze, but warns that test holds integration endpoints pointing at the payment sandbox and the email server must never send to real customers. What is a clone, and what would you configure so the clone does not cause damage?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That a clone copies a source instance's database over a target, overwriting it; that you control what is copied with exclusions and what is kept on the target with preservers; and that you plan for email, integrations and in-flight work on the target.

The Answer

A clone copies the data and configuration of a source instance (here production) onto a target instance (test). After the clone, test looks like production at the time of the snapshot. Anything on test that is not protected is lost, including unfinished update sets.

Clones are requested from the Clone Admin Console (or the older System Clone menus). The requester needs clone_admin on the source; the target must be allowed as a clone target. Exclusions, preservers and post-clone scripts are grouped in a clone profile, so make sure your request uses the right one.

  • Exclusions: tables whose data is not copied, so they arrive empty on test. ServiceNow already excludes large log, audit and notification tables by default. You might add bulky history tables testers do not need.
  • Data preservers: records on the target that are kept. Here you would preserve the test instance's REST message endpoints, connection and credential aliases, MID Server records and the instance-specific system properties that point to the payment sandbox, so test does not suddenly carry production endpoints and credentials.
  • Email: disable outbound email on the target immediately after the clone (or confirm the clone keeps it off) and check that the email redirect or test mailbox is set.
  • Before the clone: export or commit any update sets still in progress on test, warn testers, and pick a quiet window. After the clone: verify scheduled jobs and integrations on test, reset passwords if needed, and confirm data masking rules for customer data.

Common Mistakes

  • Cloning over an instance with un-exported update sets and losing weeks of work.
  • Excluding a table without preserving it, then finding it empty after the clone.
  • Letting a production integration credential land on test and having test call a live payment endpoint.
  • Cloning test over production (direction mistakes happen; double-check source and target).
Score points: Mention that preserving a table protects that table and its parents but child tables must be preserved separately, and that you would run a dry run of the profile on a lower instance first.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How often should sub-production instances be cloned, and who decides?
  • How would you mask customer personal data on the cloned instance?
  • What is the difference between excluding and preserving a table?

Sources

  • Clone Admin Console (ServiceNow docs)
  • Create a new clone preserver (ServiceNow docs)
  • ServiceNow clone made easy: a practical step-by-step (ServiceNow Community)

question: A public university's compliance office is moving its information security policy, written to ISO 27001, out of Word documents and into ServiceNow Integrated Risk Management. The compliance officer asks you to explain, in plain terms, the difference between a policy, a policy statement (control objective), a control, a risk and an issue in ServiceNow, using the rule "all staff laptops must be encrypted" as the example. What do you tell her?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A clear chain from the written rule down to the thing that is actually tested, and an understanding that controls are generated per entity (the thing in scope), not typed in by hand one by one.

The Answer

  • Policy: the governing document, here the university's Information Security Policy. It has an owner, approvers and a review cycle, and can be mapped to external authority documents such as ISO 27001.
  • Policy statement / control objective: one testable requirement inside the policy: "Staff laptops must use full-disk encryption." Newer versions label these control objectives; older material calls them policy statements. One policy holds many of them.
  • Entity and entity type: what the requirement applies to. Entity types (for example "Staff laptop" or "Faculty") with filters select entities automatically, such as each faculty's laptop fleet.
  • Control: the control objective applied to a specific entity: "Laptop encryption - Faculty of Engineering". Controls are stored in sn_compliance_control. Because they are generated from objective times entity, adding a new faculty creates its control without anyone retyping the requirement.
  • Risk: what could go wrong if the control fails: "Loss of student personal data from a stolen laptop". Risks are assessed for likelihood and impact and are linked to the controls that reduce them.
  • Issue: a recorded gap. If a control test, indicator or attestation shows the Engineering laptops are not encrypted, an issue is raised with an owner, a due date and a remediation plan.

So the chain reads: Policy, then control objective, then control per entity, which mitigates a risk; when evidence shows the control is not working, an issue is created and tracked to closure.

Common Mistakes

  • Creating one control per laptop. Entities should be meaningful units of accountability, not every device.
  • Treating a policy exception as an issue. An exception is an approved, time-limited deviation with compensating controls; an issue is an unplanned failure.
  • Typing controls by hand instead of letting entity scoping generate them.
Score points: Mention that one control objective can be mapped to several authority document citations (ISO 27001, a national data protection law), so a single test satisfies several frameworks. That "test once, comply many" idea is the main reason customers move off spreadsheets.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you collect evidence that the control works: an indicator, an attestation or a manual test?
  • Who should own the control: the faculty IT lead or central IT?
  • How do you handle a lab that cannot encrypt its specialist laptops?

Sources

  • Understanding Policy and Compliance Management in ServiceNow GRC (community)
  • Components installed with Policy and Compliance Management
  • Indicators, control and risk owner (entity owner) - GRC forum

question: A 600-person SaaS company is connecting its ServiceNow instance to Okta. The IT manager asks three things: what SAML single sign-on actually changes about how people log in, whether ServiceNow's own multi-factor authentication is still needed once Okta enforces MFA, and why the implementation partner insists on keeping two local admin accounts. How do you answer?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A plain explanation of who authenticates whom under SAML, where MFA should live, and why a controlled break-glass path matters.

The Answer

What SSO changes. With SAML 2.0, ServiceNow becomes the service provider and Okta the identity provider. When a user opens the instance, ServiceNow sends them to Okta; Okta checks the password (and MFA) and sends back a signed assertion saying who the user is. ServiceNow trusts that assertion and matches it to a user record. Passwords are no longer checked by ServiceNow, so leavers are cut off centrally the moment Okta disables them. In ServiceNow this is configured through Multi-Provider SSO, which lets one instance trust more than one IdP if the company later acquires a business with its own directory.

Is ServiceNow MFA still needed? For SSO users, MFA belongs in Okta, where it covers every application consistently. ServiceNow's own MFA (switched on with glide.authenticate.multifactor) matters for local logins, which do not pass through Okta. There is a separate property, glide.authenticate.mfa.with.multisso.enabled, for the less common case where you want ServiceNow MFA on top of SSO. Note that the MFA context policy applies to interactive user logins, not to API basic authentication, so integration accounts need their own controls such as OAuth and restricted roles.

Why keep local admins? If the IdP is down, the certificate expires or someone misconfigures SSO, nobody can log in. A small number of break-glass local accounts, with strong passwords, ServiceNow MFA, monitoring and a documented procedure, let the team recover. The community-known path is the side_door.do login page, which shows the native login form; test it after every upgrade, because SSO auto-redirect settings can affect it.

Common Mistakes

  • Leaving every user with a local password "just in case", which keeps an unmonitored login path open.
  • Forgetting the IdP signing certificate's expiry date.
  • Turning on SSO in production without testing on a sub-production instance and with a second admin session open.
Score points: Mention glide.authenticate.multisso.debug for troubleshooting SSO, and that break-glass account use should raise an alert to the security team every time.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How are new users created or updated from SAML attributes on first login?
  • How would you handle contractors who are not in Okta?
  • How do integration users authenticate if they cannot use SSO?

Sources

  • Multi-Provider SSO properties, tables, and scripts
  • Multi-factor authentication system properties
  • Side door login for SSO issues - community thread

question: A 900-bed hospital has just licensed Vulnerability Response. A new analyst on the infrastructure team has been told "the Qualys findings now land in ServiceNow" and opens the module for the first time. She sees Vulnerabilities, Vulnerable Items and Remediation Tasks and asks why ServiceNow doesn't simply raise an Incident for every scanner finding. Explain the three record types, how they relate, and why the hospital would not use Incident for this.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That you understand Vulnerability Response (VR) has its own data model with a clear separation between what the weakness is, where it exists, and who is fixing it, and that this separation is what makes scanner data usable at scale.

The Answer

  • Vulnerability is the library entry: the CVE or the scanner's own vulnerability definition (for Qualys, a QID). It describes the weakness, its scores and the solution text. It exists once, no matter how many machines are affected.
  • Vulnerable Item (VI), stored in sn_vul_vulnerable_item, is the finding: this vulnerability detected on this configuration item. VIs are created automatically by the scanner integration imports, and the CI is resolved from the scanner's host data against the CMDB. If 400 workstations have the same browser flaw, you get one Vulnerability and 400 VIs.
  • Remediation Task is the unit of work. Remediation task rules group many VIs into one task and route it to an assignment group. The base rule groups VIs by vulnerability and assignment group, so the desktop team gets one task covering all 400 workstations rather than 400 tickets.

Why not Incident? An Incident means a service is interrupted or degraded. A missing patch is a risk, not an outage. Feeding scanner output into Incident would bury the service desk in tens of thousands of records, break incident SLAs and metrics, and lose the things VR adds: risk scoring per finding, remediation target dates per risk rating, automatic closure when the next scan no longer sees the finding, exception (deferral) handling with approvals, and reporting by CI, owner group and business service.

For the hospital this matters because many devices (imaging workstations, clinical systems) cannot be patched on demand. VR lets the team defer a VI with a recorded reason and approval instead of leaving an Incident open forever.

Common Mistakes

  • Saying the remediation task is the vulnerability. Closing a task without the scanner confirming the fix leaves the VI open, which is the correct behavior.
  • Treating the CMDB as optional. If CI matching is poor, VIs are assigned to the wrong team or no team.
  • Expecting analysts to create VIs by hand. They come from the integration.
Score points: Mention that viewing VIs requires at least the sn_vul.read_all role, and that the scanner, not the assignee, is the source of truth for whether a finding is really fixed.

Likely Follow-ups

  • What happens to a VI when the next scan no longer reports the finding?
  • How would you route all VIs on clinical devices to the biomedical engineering group?
  • What is a remediation target date and where does it come from?

Sources

  • Vulnerability Response vulnerable item form fields
  • Vulnerability Response remediation tasks and remediation task rules overview
  • Qualys VMDR ITSM integration: hosts and assets

question: A national retailer has 9,000 store employees and about 1,500 contractors who run seasonal stock counts. After launching its Service Catalog, the retailer finds that contractors can see and order the "Corporate Credit Card Request" item, which should be limited to salaried head-office staff. The item's catalog category is already restricted to head office. Explain how visibility of catalog items is controlled in ServiceNow, why the category restriction did not help, and how you would fix this.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That catalog visibility is controlled by user criteria attached through Available For and Not Available For. They want to hear that Not Available For wins, that category criteria do not cascade down to items, and how to debug which criteria a user matched.

The Answer

User criteria are reusable records that describe a set of users by user, group, role, company, department, location, or an advanced script. You attach them to catalog items and categories through two related lists:

  • Available For: only users who match at least one listed criterion can see the item.
  • Not Available For: users who match are blocked. This overrides Available For, so someone who matches both cannot access the item.

Why the category restriction did not help: criteria on a category control the category itself. They are not inherited by the items in it. The credit card item had no criteria of its own, so anyone with catalog access could reach it, for example through search or a direct link.

The fix:

  1. Create (or reuse) a user criteria record such as "Head office salaried staff". Build it from a condition on department or employee type if HR data supports that, or from a group. Avoid hard-coding a list of users.
  2. Add it to the item's Available For list.
  3. Optionally, create a "Contractors" criteria record and add it to Not Available For as a safety net, because it overrides everything else.
  4. Test with impersonation, and use the user criteria diagnostics / debug user criteria view for the catalog item. It shows which criteria matched a selected user and whether each match came from Available For or Not Available For.

Two practical notes. First, changes to a user's profile apply right away to standard criteria, but scripted criteria are cached for the session, so the user may need to log out and back in. Second, user criteria restrict access inside the Service Catalog. They are not ACLs on the underlying tables, so sensitive data still needs proper ACLs.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming criteria on a category protect every item in it.
  • Writing a catalog client script that hides the item or blocks submission. That is not a security control.
  • Building scripted criteria for something a simple group or department condition can express. Scripted criteria are harder to maintain and cached per session.
  • Treating user criteria as data security for the RITM table.
Score points: Say "Not Available For overrides Available For" and "category criteria do not cascade to items" in the first minute. Then mention reusing one criteria record across many items so HR changes only need to be made in one place.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you restrict a knowledge base to the same population?
  • A user still sees an item after you added criteria. What would you check?
  • When is a scripted user criterion justified?

Sources

  • Apply user criteria to items and categories (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Debug user criteria of a catalog item (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Why does user criteria not restrict access to catalog items? (ServiceNow Community)

question: At a public university, the CIO's office gets 60+ ideas a term from faculties: a new student-advisor portal, a lab-booking app, a Wi-Fi upgrade in two halls. Today these go straight to the PMO as 'projects' and half stall. The CIO asks you: in ServiceNow Strategic Portfolio Management, what is the difference between an idea/demand and a project, and why should requests not start life as projects?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That a demand is a request for investment that still has to be assessed and approved, while a project is committed work with a plan, budget and resources. The demand stage is where the organisation says 'not now' cheaply, before people and money are tied up.

The Answer

In SPM the flow is usually idea → demand → project (or another work type).

  • Idea: a lightweight suggestion from a business user, such as a faculty member. Ideas can be converted to demands.
  • Demand (stored in dmn_demand): a structured request with business case, cost and benefit estimates, risk, and the portfolio it belongs to. The documented states are Draft, Submitted, Screening, Qualified, Approved, Deferred, Completed. In Screening, stakeholders fill in assessments that score the demand (for example strategic alignment, value, risk); scorecards show the result.
  • Project: created from an approved demand. The demand's Category and Type decide what gets created: a project, an enhancement, or an Enterprise Agile Planning item for agile teams. Demand data carries over so nobody re-types it.

Why not start as projects:

  • Comparison: demands can be compared side by side (value vs cost vs risk) so the university funds the best 15 ideas, not the loudest 60.
  • Capacity honesty: a project implies resources. Creating 60 projects means 60 teams asking for the same architects, which is why half stall.
  • Cheap 'no': deferring a demand costs nothing. Cancelling a half-run project wastes money and goodwill.
  • Right work type: the Wi-Fi upgrade might be a standard change or an enhancement to an existing service, not a project at all.

For the university, a sensible setup is: faculties submit demands through a portal form; a demand manager screens them; a governance board reviews scored, qualified demands each term; approved ones become projects or agile work.

Common Mistakes

  • Letting every request skip screening because 'the dean asked'.
  • Designing a 40-question assessment nobody completes. Keep scoring short and consistent.
  • Treating demand approval as the end. Benefits should be checked after delivery.
Score points: Mention that the demand's Category and Type decide whether it becomes a project, an enhancement or agile work.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Who should approve demands, and how often should the board meet?
  • How would you score a demand that is mandatory for compliance?
  • How does a demand feed capacity planning before it is approved?

Sources

  • Demand workflow (ServiceNow docs)
  • Use Demand Management (ServiceNow docs)

question: A European telco's service desk gets about 9,000 incidents a month across 70 assignment groups. Around 30% are first assigned to the wrong group and bounce at least once. They already own Predictive Intelligence. The service desk manager wants new incidents from the portal to be auto-routed to the right group. How do you build it, and how do you decide whether the model is good enough to switch on?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Start from the OOTB Incident Assignment classification solution, train on clean closed data, judge it per class using precision and coverage, and only auto-apply predictions where confidence is high. Recognise that bad training data (the 30% mis-routing) can teach the model the same mistakes.

The Answer

1. Check prerequisites. Classification for incidents needs the Predictive Intelligence plugins (com.glide.platform_ml and the incident ML solution plugin). With those active, ServiceNow ships template solution definitions: Incident Assignment, Incident Categorization, Incident Service and Incident Configuration Item. You need admin or ml_admin.

2. Configure the solution definition (Predictive Intelligence > Classification > Solution Definitions):

  • Table: Incident. Output field: Assignment group.
  • Input fields: what the caller actually fills in at creation, usually Short description (plus Description or Category if reliably populated). Do not use fields that are set after routing, or the model learns from the answer.
  • Filter: inactive, resolved or closed incidents, with a relative date range (for example the last 12 months), and exclude reassigned tickets or use the final resolving group so the 30% mistakes do not become training truth. Docs recommend roughly 30,000 to 300,000 records; at 9,000 a month, 12 months is enough.
  • Training frequency: run once while tuning, then schedule retraining (for example every 30 days) because groups and services change.

Classes with fewer than 30 training records are excluded, so tiny groups will never be predicted. That is acceptable; they stay manual.

3. Evaluate. After training, look at the Class Confidence section of Solution Statistics and the per-class precision/coverage chart. Precision = how often a prediction is correct; coverage = how often the model is confident enough to predict at all. Use the Test Solutions tab with real short descriptions. You can tune each class to a different precision/coverage point, for example high precision for the Network Core group where a wrong route is costly.

4. Apply predictions. Use a before-insert business rule on incident that calls the Predictive Intelligence prediction API for your solution (ServiceNow ships a prediction business rule template you can copy), or use the prediction in a flow. Apply only when the result is above the class threshold; otherwise leave the incident with the service desk triage group. The OOTB Update Prediction Results business rule updates precision/coverage statistics when an incident is closed, which gives you real-world accuracy over time.

5. Go/no-go. Agree a bar with the manager up front, for example: at least 80% precision on predicted tickets and at least 50% coverage, measured on a pilot of two weeks. Track reassignment count before and after.

Common Mistakes

  • Training on all incidents, including open ones with no final group.
  • Hard-coding dates in the filter so the training window never moves.
  • Auto-assigning every prediction regardless of confidence.
  • Using a generative AI skill when a cheap, proven classifier does the job.
Score points: Point out that the reassignment problem can poison training data, and say how you filter for the group that actually resolved the ticket.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Coverage is only 35%. What do you change first?
  • How would you handle a re-organisation that merges 10 groups next month?
  • When would you add similarity (similar incidents) instead of, or in addition to, classification?

Sources

  • Create and train a classification solution (ServiceNow docs)
  • Predictive Intelligence for Incident Management (ServiceNow docs)

question: A mid-size insurance company built a scoped app for property claims (custom table, about 40 fields, long adjuster notes). Adjusters spend 10-15 minutes reading a claim before calling the customer. None of the OOTB Now Assist skills cover this table. The business asks for a 'Summarize claim' button. How would you build it with Now Assist Skill Kit, and what would you check before turning it on?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The Skill Kit lifecycle (create, inputs, tools, prompt, test, deployment settings, publish, activate), a grounded prompt that only uses record data, and the non-functional checks: privacy masking, guardrails, cost, and measurement. Knowing that newer docs call it AI Skill Kit under the ServiceNow Otto brand is a plus.

The Answer

Create the skill. With the sn_skill_builder.admin role, open Now Assist Skill Kit > Home > Create new skill. Give it a name and description, and pick the provider. Docs list Now LLM Service plus external options such as Azure OpenAI, Google Gemini and Anthropic Claude on AWS; which providers are allowed can be governed centrally. Build it in the claims app scope.

Inputs and tools. Define an input of type record for the claim. Add tool nodes to collect what the prompt needs: a script tool that returns a compact JSON of the fields that matter (policy type, loss date, reserve, status, last 10 adjuster notes), or a retriever for policy wording. Tools run in sequence by default; decision nodes can route between tools. Trim the data: sending all 40 fields and every note wastes tokens and adds noise.

Prompt. Write instructions that are specific to the job:

  • Role and audience: 'You are summarising a property claim for the adjuster before a customer call.'
  • Structure: loss summary, coverage status, open actions, risks, customer sentiment, in under 150 words.
  • Grounding: 'Use only the provided data. If a field is missing, say Not recorded. Do not infer coverage decisions.'

Test. Run the skill against 20-30 real claims of different types (simple, litigated, large loss). Have two senior adjusters grade them for accuracy and missing facts. Iterate on the prompt and the tool output, not just the wording.

Deployment settings. In Skill settings > Deployment settings, choose where it appears. Options include the Now Assist panel, a UI action, a flow action, the context menu, the virtual assistant and UI Builder. For a 'Summarize claim' button, a UI action on the claim form (or the workspace) fits. Then publish, and activate it in the Now Assist Admin console for the adjuster role only. A published skill can also be called from a flow through the Execute Skill action.

Before go-live check:

  • Privacy: Data Privacy for Now Assist can mask PII patterns before the prompt leaves the instance and restore them in the response. Confirm the policy covers claim-specific data like policy numbers and bank details.
  • Guardrails: per the AI Guardian FAQ, prompt injection detection is not on by default for custom skills; configure it for this skill. Adjuster notes can contain text pasted from emails.
  • Access: the script tool must respect ACLs; do not read data with elevated rights that the adjuster cannot see.
  • Consumption and value: estimate calls per day against your assist entitlement, and baseline the 10-15 minute reading time so you can show the saving.

Common Mistakes

  • Dumping the whole record into the prompt.
  • Testing on three hand-picked claims.
  • Forgetting to activate the skill in the admin console after publishing, then debugging a 'missing button'.
Score points: Say you would update the Generative AI Controller together with the Skill Kit, and that the skill should never make the coverage decision, only summarise.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Adjusters say the summary sometimes invents a settlement amount. How do you fix it?
  • How would you reuse this skill inside an AI agent?
  • How do you move the skill from dev to prod?

Sources

  • Now Assist Skill Kit / AI Skill Kit (ServiceNow docs)
  • Add a tool to a skill (ServiceNow docs)
  • Configure skill deployment settings (ServiceNow docs)
  • AI Guardian FAQ (ServiceNow Community)

question: A state government procurement office routes purchase requests for approval based on amount, category (IT, facilities, professional services), funding source (state, federal grant) and agency. Today that logic is a 120-line If/Else script in a flow, and policy changes every fiscal year require a developer and a release. The procurement policy team wants to maintain the rules themselves. How would you redesign this in Workflow Studio?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Move the rules out of code into a decision table, call it from the flow with Make a decision, and give the policy team a safe way to edit and publish rules (drafts, testing, access). Interviewers also want to hear what still belongs in the flow.

The Answer

1. Model the decision. Inputs: amount (number/currency), category (choice), funding source (choice), agency (reference). Result: the approval path, for example a reference to an approver group or a choice like 'Manager only', 'Manager + Finance', 'Manager + Finance + Grants Office'. List the current rules from the script as rows and check them with the policy team before building. You will usually find dead rules and overlaps.

2. Build the decision table in Workflow Studio: add condition columns for each input, add a row per rule (for example: amount > 50,000 AND funding = federal grant → Manager + Finance + Grants Office), add a default 'otherwise' row, then test with sample inputs and publish. ServiceNow describes decision tables as a way to decouple decision logic from code so a business SME can maintain it.

3. Call it from the flow. Use the Make a decision flow logic and select the table. Two options:

  • Branches on: each answer gets its own path in the flow, useful when each path has different steps.
  • Branches off: answers come back as data pills, which is cleaner here. Pass the result into a single Ask for Approval step (or a subflow that loops through approval levels).
  • Choose first match for mutually exclusive rules, or all matches if several approvals can apply at once. Always configure the Otherwise path.

4. Hand over to the policy team. Give them access to edit the decision table only, not the flow. Use draft authoring so changes are tested before publishing; the docs note that for tables without draft authoring, edits are live immediately, which is risky in government procurement. Agree a simple change process (who can publish, who reviews) so there is a record of every rule change for auditors.

5. What stays in the flow: the approval mechanics, notifications, timeouts, escalations, and what happens after approval. The decision table answers 'who', the flow handles 'how'.

Common Mistakes

  • Copying the 120-line script into one giant row set without cleaning it up.
  • Encoding approver names in rows instead of groups, so the table breaks when people move.
  • No default row, so unusual requests silently go nowhere.
  • Letting SMEs edit the flow instead of the table.
Score points: Mention testing the table with boundary values (exactly 50,000) and that creating a table inline from the flow only builds the structure; rules are added in the table itself.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Two rules match the same request. How does the table decide?
  • How would you report on which rules are used most?
  • How do you promote rule changes between dev and prod, or should SMEs edit in prod?

Sources

  • Decision tables workflow (ServiceNow docs)
  • Make a decision flow logic (ServiceNow docs)
  • General guidelines for Workflow Studio flows, subflows, and actions (ServiceNow docs)

question: A mid-sized bank receives a weekly CSV of 4,000 branch ATMs and kiosk PCs from its hardware vendor. The previous admin built a transform map that coalesces on the name field, and the CMDB now has about 700 duplicate computers because the vendor sometimes changes naming conventions. The bank wants the weekly load to stop creating duplicates. How do you rebuild the import so it respects CMDB identification rules?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That coalescing in a transform map bypasses the Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE), that the supported fix is to route the import through IRE with CMDBTransformUtil, and that you also clean up the existing duplicates and set reconciliation so a weekly vendor file does not overwrite better data from Discovery.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Does the file contain a stable unique key such as serial number or asset tag?
  • Does Discovery or an endpoint tool (for example SCCM) also populate these devices?
  • Which fields is the vendor authoritative for (warranty, model, location) and which are not?

Approach

  1. Check the identification rule. In CI Class Manager, confirm the rule for the target class (for example cmdb_ci_computer or a subclass). The base hardware rule tries serial number first, then other identifier entries. Make sure the CSV maps serial number into the payload; name should be a lower-priority entry, not the only one.
  2. Remove the coalesce. Coalescing makes the transform map decide insert versus update on its own, ignoring IRE.
  3. Add an onBefore transform script that sends each row through IRE and then tells the transform to skip its own insert:
(function runTransformScript(source, map, log, target) {
    var cmdbUtil = new CMDBTransformUtil();
    cmdbUtil.setDataSource('ImportSet');
    cmdbUtil.identifyAndReconcileEnhanced(source, map, log);
    ignore = true; // IRE already wrote the CI; do not let the transform insert again

    if (cmdbUtil.hasError()) {
        log.error('IRE error: ' + cmdbUtil.getError());
    } else {
        log.info('IRE output: ' + cmdbUtil.getOutputPayload());
        log.info('CI sys_id: ' + cmdbUtil.getOutputRecordSysId());
    }
})(source, map, log, target);

CMDBTransformUtil builds the IRE payload from your field maps, so your field mapping still matters. Use one transform map per import set when using this API. The data source string must be a valid value of the discovery_source choice list on cmdb_ci; if the bank wants "ATM Vendor" as its own source for reconciliation, add that choice value and pass it instead of ImportSet.

  1. Set reconciliation rules so the vendor source can update warranty and model fields but not, for example, IP address or OS fields owned by Discovery.
  2. Clean up the 700 existing duplicates. Once identification is correct, IRE and CMDB Health raise de-duplication tasks (reconcile_duplicate_task). Work them with the Duplicate CI Remediator or de-duplication templates for bulk cases, choosing which CI survives and merging related records.
  3. Test with a sub-production run of last week's file and check the transform log for INSERT versus UPDATE counts before going live.

Common Mistakes

  • Keeping coalesce on name and adding a script to "check for duplicates". That re-implements IRE badly.
  • Forgetting ignore = true, which makes the transform insert a second record after IRE already handled it.
  • Bulk-deleting duplicates with a background script and orphaning incidents, assets and relationships.
Score points: Mention that identifyAndReconcileEnhanced supports partial payloads and duplicate handling within a batch, and that for any new vendor feed of size you would consider IntegrationHub ETL, which uses IRE natively.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you test what IRE will do without committing anything?
  • Which fields would you make the vendor authoritative for, and how?
  • When would IntegrationHub ETL be a better choice than a transform map?

Sources

  • CMDBTransformUtil API reference - ServiceNow Docs
  • Applying CI Identification and Reconciliation to Import Sets - ServiceNow Docs
  • Remediate a de-duplication task - ServiceNow Docs

question: A medical device manufacturer sells imaging equipment to 600 hospitals under three support contracts: Platinum (4-hour response, 24x7, phone and web), Gold (8 business hours, phone and web) and Standard (2 business days, web only, capped at 20 cases a year). Today agents check a spreadsheet to see what each hospital is owed. How would you configure Customer Service Management so the right entitlement and SLA apply to each case automatically?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Correct use of contracts, entitlements and SLA definitions, with the entitlement check at case creation, unit-based tracking, and channel restrictions. The candidate should prefer OOTB behaviour and say where a small customisation is really required.

Approach

  1. Model the contracts. In Customer Contracts and Entitlements, create a contract per hospital. It holds the account, covered products or assets, and the term. Load them from the ERP or CPQ system rather than by hand.
  2. Create entitlements. An entitlement defines the level of support and the allowed channels. It can be tied to an account, contract, product or asset. For each tier:
    • Platinum: phone and web channels, 24x7 schedule.
    • Gold: phone and web, business-hours schedule.
    • Standard: web only, unit type cases, total units 20.
    Only active entitlements can be picked when a case is created, so expiry is controlled by the active flag and dates.
  3. Use the entitlement check. When a case is opened, CSM runs an entitlement check against the account, product, asset and contract. That fills the case's entitlement without the agent opening a spreadsheet. If none is found, the case shows that, and the agent follows an agreed "no entitlement" path, such as paid support or a goodwill override with approval.
  4. Count usage. For case-based units, the OOTB business rule "Update case entitlement on Close" decreases remaining units when a case closes. If the customer later wants hours-based support, the docs say you need your own business rule for hours. That is a reasonable, small customisation.
  5. Create SLA definitions on the case table, one response and one resolution SLA per tier, with the right schedule:
    • Start condition matches the tier, for example on the case's entitlement or contract.
    • Platinum uses a 24x7 schedule. Gold and Standard use the business-hours schedule.
    • Response and resolution SLAs are evaluated separately. If only one attaches, check that definition's start condition.
  6. Enforce channels. Standard customers can't open cases by phone. Have agents see the entitlement channels on the case, and redirect phone callers to the portal rather than hard-blocking the call.
