question: A hospital network (25,000 staff, 14 sites) turned on Now Assist in AI Search for its employee portal. Within a month: nurses report answers quoting an infection-control procedure that was replaced in March; a facilities question returned a summary citing an HR-only article; and 40% of generated answers get a thumbs-down. Clinical governance wants it switched off. Question: How do you diagnose these three problems and what do you change, without simply turning the feature off?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That generated search answers are only as good as the indexed content and the configuration (search profile, sources, access) behind them. The LLM summarises what retrieval gives it; most 'AI problems' here are knowledge-management and access problems. A candidate should treat the HR-article case as a potential data exposure first.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Did the user who saw the HR article actually have read access to it through user criteria or ACLs? Was the article only cited, or was the content shown?
  • Which search profile and Genius Result configuration does the portal use? Are legacy Q&A Genius Results still active alongside the Multi-Content Response?
  • Is the old infection-control article retired, or still published with a newer duplicate?
  • What do the thumbs-down comments say: wrong, outdated, not relevant, too long?

Approach

Problem 2 first: the HR article (possible exposure). Reproduce it by impersonating the facilities user. AI Search applies access controls to results; if the user can see the article, the problem is the article's user criteria or knowledge base permissions, not the AI. Check whether the HR knowledge base has 'can read' criteria limited to HR, and whether someone added 'Any user' to an article. If the user could not open the article but the answer cited it, treat it as a defect and raise it with ServiceNow support. Either way, inform clinical governance with facts, not guesses.

Problem 1: outdated procedure. Now Assist Multi-Content Response constrains the LLM context to indexed content and returns citations. If the March replacement exists but the old article is still published, both are retrievable and the model may use the older one. Fix the content: retire the old version, set valid-to dates, and make sure the knowledge workflow retires superseded articles. Check that the index is current after the change. For clinical content, consider scoping clinical procedures to a dedicated knowledge base with a strict owner and review cycle.

Problem 3: 40% negative feedback. Pull a sample of 100 thumbs-down interactions and classify them:

  • Retrieval misses (right answer not found): improve synonyms and stop words in the search profile, article titles and short descriptions; add missing content.
  • Wrong source type: limit the search sources in the portal's search profile to what staff need (knowledge, catalog), and remove noisy sources.
  • Answer format: long or vague answers usually come from long, multi-topic articles. Split articles into one topic each.
  • Legacy configs: the Multi-Content Response replaces the legacy Now Assist Q&A and Actions Genius Results configurations; if those legacy configurations are still active and fire first in the profile order, they can compete with the multi-content answer.

Governance response. Instead of switching off, propose: take the clinical knowledge base out of the portal's generated answers for two weeks while content is cleaned (for example by narrowing the search source conditions on that profile, and keeping clinical content findable through normal search elsewhere), keep generated answers on for IT and facilities, and report weekly feedback rates. Enable AI Guardian offensiveness logging where supported, and keep Data Privacy masking on.

Trade-offs

  • Excluding clinical content lowers risk but also lowers usefulness for nurses, the largest user group.
  • Tight user criteria protect data but make retrieval sparser; that is the right side to err on in a hospital.
  • Splitting articles improves answers but is real editorial work; prioritise the top 200 searched articles.

Common Mistakes

  • Blaming the LLM and tuning prompts when the index contains two conflicting procedures.
  • Testing as admin, which hides access issues.
  • Turning the feature off without fixing the knowledge base, so the same problems hit the next rollout.
Score points: Say 'garbage in, garbage summarised': the fix is knowledge lifecycle (retirement, ownership, one topic per article) plus access hygiene, with the AI layer last.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you measure answer quality over time, beyond thumbs up/down?
  • Clinical governance asks for a guarantee the AI will never cite a retired article. What can you honestly commit to?
  • How would you add documents from SharePoint to the same experience?

Sources

  • Now Assist Multi-Content Response Genius Results (ServiceNow docs)
  • Genius Results in AI Search (ServiceNow docs)
  • Now Assist Guardian (ServiceNow docs)

question: An airline built a scoped app to track crew certifications (42,000 active records). A nightly scheduled flow does Look Up Records on all of them, loops with For Each, checks each expiry date, creates a reminder task and sends an email if expiry is within 30 days. The flow now runs over three hours, is sometimes cancelled, approvals in other flows are delayed every morning, and some crew get duplicate reminders. Question: Diagnose what is wrong and redesign it.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That the flow does the filtering in the wrong place (in a loop, not in the query), exceeds ServiceNow's documented design limits, and has no idempotency, so retries create duplicates. A strong answer redesigns for 'only touch what changed' and explains when a flow is still the right tool.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • How many records actually fall inside the 30-day window on a typical night? (Usually a few hundred, not 42,000.)
  • Is flow reporting turned on in production? What priority is the flow set to?
  • Does a reminder need to go once, or every N days until renewed?
  • Are the duplicates from the same run or from a re-run after cancellation?

Approach

Diagnosis

  • Looping over everything. ServiceNow's flow guidelines say to avoid more than about 1,000 items in one For Each, and the iteration cap property sn_flow_designer.max_iterations defaults to 1,000 and should not be raised. Large loops also cause memory pressure from storing execution context.
  • Long runtime. The guidance treats flows running longer than about an hour as too long; they should be split.
  • Shared engine contention. A heavy flow competes for the same flow engine workers as approvals and catalog flows. If it was set to high priority 'to finish faster', it makes the morning delays worse; the guidance is low priority for high-volume, non-urgent flows.
  • Reporting overhead. If flow reporting is on in production, every iteration writes execution detail. The docs recommend turning it off in production.
  • Duplicates. Nothing records that a reminder was sent, so a re-run (or overlapping runs) repeats work.

Redesign

  1. Filter in the query, not the loop. Look Up Records with conditions: active is true, expiry date on or before 30 days from now (relative condition), and 'reminder sent' is false (or 'last reminder date' older than 7 days). Set a maximum on Look Up Records. This turns 42,000 iterations into a few hundred.
  2. Make it idempotent. Add a 'last reminder sent' date on the certification. The subflow sets it in the same step that creates the task. A re-run then finds nothing to do. Also check for an existing open reminder task before creating one.
  3. Move the per-record work to a subflow ('Send certification reminder', input: certification record). The parent loop only calls it. Reuse it from the crew manager's 'remind now' UI action.
  4. Spread the load. If volume can still exceed about 1,000 (for example after a regulatory change), run the scheduled flow more often over smaller slices, or batch by base or fleet.
  5. Flow settings. Low priority, reporting off in production, error handler that logs the failing certification and continues.
  6. Consider event-driven instead of nightly. A record trigger when expiry date is set, plus a 'Wait for a duration' until 30 days before expiry, sounds elegant but leaves 42,000 waiting flow contexts for months. The guidance is to avoid flows that wait indefinitely. A daily filtered scheduled flow is the better design here.

Notification design. Send one digest per crew member if they have several expiring certificates, and a daily summary to crew scheduling instead of one email per record.

Trade-offs

  • Scheduled filtered flow: simple, visible to admins, easy to re-run. Slight delay (up to a day).
  • Script in a scheduled job with GlideRecord: faster for very high volumes, but less visible to low-code maintainers. Justified only if the flow approach still cannot keep up.
  • Long waits per record: real-time precision, but heavy on the engine and fragile across upgrades and data changes.

Common Mistakes

  • Raising sn_flow_designer.max_iterations to 50,000.
  • Setting the flow to high priority.
  • Fixing duplicates by deleting tasks after the fact instead of making the flow idempotent.
  • Using gs.sleep() in scripts to 'pace' work; the guidance says use flow logic or waits instead.
Score points: Quote the roughly 1,000-iteration and one-hour guidance, and lead with 'filter at the database, not in the loop'. Idempotency is the senior signal.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you prove the redesign fixed the morning approval delays?
  • Crew managers want to see why a reminder was not sent. What do you log and where?
  • When would you choose a scheduled script over a flow for this?

Sources

  • General guidelines for Workflow Studio flows, subflows, and actions (ServiceNow docs)
  • For Each flow logic (ServiceNow docs)

question:
An airline has three sources writing to the same 9,000 Windows servers: ServiceNow Discovery (nightly), a Service Graph Connector for Microsoft SCCM (every 6 hours), and server engineers who edit records by hand. In the last month the OS version on 1,100 servers flipped back and forth between Discovery and SCCM values, change approvers were routed to the wrong group because someone's manual edit to the support group was overwritten, and a CAB rejected two changes because the CI 'looked wrong'.
Question: Diagnose what is going on and design the reconciliation model. Explain how IRE decides who wins, and what you would configure.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That this is not an identification problem (the CIs are matched correctly) but a reconciliation problem: multiple authorised sources update the same attributes with no defined precedence. The candidate should explain reconciliation rules, priority, the static versus dynamic option, data refresh behaviour, and how manual edits fit in, then propose an attribute-level ownership model.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Which values are actually right? For OS version, is SCCM more current because the agent sees patch-level details, or is Discovery more reliable?
  • Are any reconciliation rules defined today for cmdb_ci_win_server or its parents?
  • What is the SCCM connector writing as its source, and are the engineers editing via the form, a list edit or an import?
  • Which fields must humans own (support group, change group, business criticality)?

Diagnosis

  • With no reconciliation rules for an attribute, any source can update it, so the last writer wins. Discovery runs nightly, SCCM every 6 hours, which is exactly the flip-flopping seen.
  • Reconciliation only applies to updates through IRE. Discovery and the SCCM connector both use IRE, but a manual form edit does not go through IRE, so the next automated run can overwrite it unless that attribute is excluded from those sources' authority.
  • Look at the CI's history and the discovery_source field, and the CI's activity history to confirm which source wrote last and when.

Design

  1. Build an attribute ownership matrix with the server team, for example:
    • OS, OS version, CPU, RAM, IP: Discovery priority 100, SCCM priority 200 (fallback when Discovery fails to log in).
    • Installed software and patch level: SCCM first.
    • Support group, change group, managed by, environment: not writable by Discovery or SCCM at all. Owned by humans or, better, by the service instance/offering sync.
  2. Create reconciliation rules per class and attribute (CI Class Manager > Reconciliation). Lower priority numbers win. Once any reconciliation rule exists for an attribute, only sources listed in rules for that attribute may update it. Define rules at cmdb_ci_server or cmdb_ci_computer if they should apply broadly; child class rules override parent rules.
  3. Handle staleness. Pure priority means a dead Discovery credential could freeze OS version forever. Add a data refresh rule (or equivalent stale-after setting on the reconciliation configuration) so that if the higher-priority source has not updated the attribute within, say, 7 days, the next source is allowed to update it.
  4. Consider dynamic reconciliation for attributes where the "most reported" value is a better signal than a fixed ranking. Only one dynamic rule is allowed per class attribute, and for two sources it rarely helps; it is more useful with three or more feeds.
  5. Use Preview Rule and Recompute. Preview shows the effective precedence per attribute; Recompute recalculates existing values after rules change instead of waiting for the next run.
  6. Lock down manual edits on discovered attributes (read-only via ACL or UI policy for non-CMDB-admins) and move group ownership to CSDM: support and change groups on the service offering, pushed to CIs through dynamic CI group synchronisation.

Trade-offs

  • Strict priority is predictable but can freeze data when the top source fails; refresh rules add a time element that makes behaviour harder to explain.
  • Making fields read-only reduces errors but needs a fast path (a request or a CMDB data correction task) so engineers are not blocked.
  • Defining rules at a parent class is less work but can surprise teams that own child classes with different data sources.

Common Mistakes

  • Turning off one source to "stop the fight", losing data that source was best at.
  • Assuming reconciliation rules affect inserts; they only govern updates.
  • Defining a rule for Discovery only and forgetting that this silently blocks every other source from that attribute.
Score points: Tie the CAB symptom back to data ownership: approvers trust a CI when they can see which source owns each attribute and that it was refreshed recently. Show them the Preview Rule output.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you prove to the server team that the rules work before turning them on in production?
  • What would you do if a third source, a cloud connector, starts writing the same servers?
  • How do source_native_key and source_recency_timestamp help with partial payloads?

Sources

  • Reconciliation rules - ServiceNow Docs
  • Create a CI reconciliation rule - ServiceNow Docs
  • Components and process of Identification and Reconciliation - ServiceNow Docs
  • Query on Data Precedence Rules and Reconciliation Rules - ServiceNow Community

question:
A SaaS company runs about 25,000 cloud VMs that are created and destroyed by autoscaling. Cloud Discovery marks terminated instances, but 18,000 of them still sit in the CMDB as non-operational records, list views are slow, and the security team's vulnerability reports keep flagging hosts that no longer exist. An engineer proposes a nightly background script that deletes any VM not seen for 7 days.
Question: What would you recommend instead? Design the CI lifecycle and clean-up process, including how to protect records you must keep.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That deleting CIs with a script is risky (orphaned incidents, changes, vulnerabilities and relationships; no audit; no approval) and that the supported approach is CMDB Data Manager with retirement definitions and Retire, Archive and Delete policies, plus an exclusion list and dependent CI handling.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Are there compliance rules on how long infrastructure records must be kept (for example for audit or security investigations)?
  • Do incidents, changes or vulnerability items reference these VMs?
  • How does Cloud Discovery currently mark them: operational status, install status, or both?
  • Who owns these CIs (Managed by group) and would approve policy tasks?

Recommended Design

  1. Retirement definitions per class. CMDB Data Manager needs an active retirement definition for each class targeted by Retire, Archive or Delete policies, for example virtual machine instance: retired when install status is Retired and operational status is Non-Operational.
  2. Retire policy. Targets VMs that Discovery has marked terminated or not seen within the agreed window and sets them to the retired state. This removes them from operational views and from vulnerability scope without destroying history.
  3. Archive policy. After, say, 30 days retired, archive the CIs. Archived records move to archive tables, drop out of active lists and processes, and can be restored during the retention period. This is what fixes list performance.
  4. Delete policy after the retention period (for example 12 months) for records that have no audit value. Archive and Delete only act on CIs already in the retired state defined for their class. Deletion is irreversible.
  5. Exclusions. Add CIs that must never be processed automatically (for example VMs under legal hold or referenced by an open security investigation) to the CI exclusion list.
  6. Dependent CIs. When a VM is retired, its dependent CIs (network adapters, disks, software instances) can be cascaded. The tasks are generated for review unless you clear Needs Review on the policy.
  7. Approval model. Start with Needs Review on so the Managed By group approves tasks; once a few weeks of results look right, turn off review for the high-volume VM class so it runs hands-free from the daily scheduled job.
  8. Related entries. Use the Delete CMDB Related Entry policy for related non-CMDB records that would become orphaned.

Why Not the Script

  • No approval or audit trail of what was removed and why.
  • References break: incidents and changes point to empty CIs; relationships are left dangling.
  • A Discovery outage for a week would delete thousands of live VMs.
  • It repeats logic that a supported, upgrade-safe product already provides.

Trade-offs

  • Archiving keeps history but needs storage and an agreed retention period.
  • Immediate deletion is simplest for short-lived autoscaling nodes, but you lose evidence for security incidents; most organisations retire quickly and delete late.
  • Turning off review increases speed but relies heavily on correct retirement definitions.

Common Mistakes

  • Creating a Delete policy without a retirement definition and wondering why nothing happens.
  • Using CMDB Health staleness as the sole trigger without a safety check for Discovery failures.
  • Forgetting that a retired CI can still be referenced by open tasks.
  • Not telling the security team: vulnerability scanner integrations should match on operational CIs only, or retired VMs keep reappearing in reports.

Rollout

Run the Retire policy first against a small class filter (for example one cloud account) with review switched on, compare the generated tasks with what the cloud console shows as terminated, and only then widen the filter. Once retirement has run cleanly for a month, enable Archive, and enable Delete last. This staged order means any mistake in a retirement definition is caught while it is still fully reversible.

Score points: Separate the problem into three outcomes, each with its own policy: out of operations (retire), out of the way (archive), and out of the database (delete).

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you guard against a Discovery outage causing a mass retirement?
  • Should short-lived autoscaling nodes be in the CMDB at all? What is the alternative?
  • How would you report on how many CIs each policy processed per month?

Sources

  • Retirement definitions - ServiceNow Docs
  • Dependent CIs management - ServiceNow Docs
  • CMDB Health KPIs and metrics - ServiceNow Docs

question: A card payments processor serves 120 partner banks, and through them roughly 90,000 merchants (shops and restaurants). Merchants raise terminal and settlement issues. Some banks want to handle their merchants' cases themselves; others want the processor to deal with merchants directly. Each bank must only see its own merchants, and a merchant must never see another merchant's data. The previous consultant proposed making every merchant a consumer. Question: how would you model banks and merchants in CSM, control portal visibility, and what are the trade-offs of the consumer proposal?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Strong understanding of the CSM account model (accounts, contacts, partner accounts, hierarchies, relationships), the external roles that drive portal visibility, and an honest view of the consumer option. This is the kind of B2B2B question practitioners still debate on the Community, so a structured trade-off matters more than one "right" answer.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Is a merchant always one legal business with staff, or are many sole traders?
  • Do merchants have contracts and entitlements with the processor, or only with their bank?
  • Which banks want to work cases versus only view them?
  • How are terminals tracked: as assets or install base items tied to the merchant?
  • Can a merchant move from one bank to another?

Recommended Model

  • Banks are accounts flagged as partners. CSM accounts can be customers, partners, or both, in [customer_account].
  • Merchants are customer accounts, with their staff as contacts in [customer_contact]. A merchant is a business with several people, terminals and entitlements, which is what accounts are designed for.
  • Link each merchant to its bank with a partner relationship, rather than making merchants child accounts of the bank. A hierarchy says "is part of", which is not true legally. A partner relationship says "is supported by", and it can change when a merchant switches bank.
  • Roles for the portal:
    • Bank staff who work merchant cases get sn_customerservice.partner. Partners can create and manage cases for the customer accounts they support and see their assets.
    • Bank leads get sn_customerservice.partner_admin to manage contacts and cases across their merchants.
    • Merchant owners get sn_customerservice.customer_admin for their own account. Other merchant staff get sn_customerservice.customer.
  • Two service patterns. For banks that self-serve, cases route to the bank's partner contacts first and escalate to the processor. For direct banks, merchants log cases with the processor and the bank gets read visibility. Drive this from an attribute on the partner relationship or the bank account, not from separate code paths.
  • Terminals as assets or install base items on the merchant account. That supports entitlement checks and proactive outage notifications later.

Trade-offs of the Consumer Proposal

  • For it: simpler login for sole-trader merchants and fewer records. The household concept is irrelevant here, though.
  • Against it: a consumer is an individual. A restaurant with a manager and three shift leads needs multiple people sharing visibility of one set of cases, which accounts and contacts give you for free. Partner access to consumers is not the natural pattern; partner roles are built around supported accounts. Asset, contract and entitlement reporting by merchant also becomes awkward.
  • Middle ground: merchants as accounts by default. If a large group of true sole traders exists, model them as accounts with a single contact. The structure stays the same, so you don't run two models.

Visibility Testing

Build a persona matrix covering bank A partner, bank A partner admin, bank B partner, merchant 1 admin, merchant 1 staff and merchant 2 admin. For each, check cases, contacts, assets and knowledge. Include list views and portal search as well as forms. Community reports show that list visibility for external roles can behave differently from what people expect.

Trade-offs

  • Partner relationships are flexible but add a dependency on relationship data quality. A merchant with no bank link is invisible to the bank.
  • 90,000 merchant accounts is fine for the platform, but onboarding them needs automation from the processor's merchant system, not manual creation.
  • Customising ACLs per bank is tempting but should be the last resort after OOTB roles and relationships.

Common Mistakes

  • Putting merchants under banks in the account hierarchy, then struggling when a merchant changes bank.
  • Creating one portal per bank instead of one portal with role-driven visibility.
  • Testing visibility only as an internal admin.
Score points: Call out data protection. Payment card data must never land in case descriptions or attachments. Propose data masking or a sensitive-data detection rule on inbound email and portal forms.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a merchant chain with 400 outlets?
  • How would a bank's own ServiceNow instance exchange cases with yours?
  • Which reports would each bank see, and how do you keep them scoped?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: Roles installed with Customer Service Management
  • ServiceNow Docs: Customer data
  • ServiceNow Community: Financial institutions and merchants in CSM

question: A SaaS company runs a multi-tenant HR software platform for 2,300 business customers. Last month a database failover took the EU region down for 95 minutes. Customers opened 640 cases in the first hour, the support portal slowed, agents typed the same reply over and over, and 30 enterprise customers complained they heard nothing until they raised a case. The company already uses ITOM Event Management and Service Mapping internally, and CSM for support. Question: how would you redesign outage handling so customers are told before they call, and support isn't flooded?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That the candidate connects ITOM and CSM through Proactive Customer Service Operations, knows the install base concept, knows how alerts map to affected customers and proactive cases, and uses major issue management for many customers at once. The answer should also cover communication, deflection and how to prove it worked.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Is each customer's tenant or region recorded anywhere, and do service maps model the EU region as its own service?
  • Are customers' subscriptions recorded as install base items in CSM?
  • Which customers have contractual outage-notification obligations?
  • How noisy is Event Management today? Would auto-creating cases from every alert be dangerous?

Diagnosis

The company had all the signals but no link from the infrastructure alert to the customers affected. Support learned about the outage from customer cases, which is backwards.

Design

  1. Install base. Record what each customer consumes, for example "HR Suite - EU region - tenant 4411", as install base items on the customer account, linked to the service CIs from Service Mapping. This is the foundation; without it nothing below works.
  2. Proactive Customer Service Operations (plugin com.snc.proactive_cs_itom). It connects CSM with the Event Management console:
    • Event Management works out the impacted services (CIs) for each alert and records them in its impacted-CI table.
    • The alert form's Affected Install Base related list shows the customer install base items tied to those services. The Refresh Affected Install Base Items action recalculates it.
    • Operators can create proactive cases from the alert by hand. If the Create Proactive Case rule is enabled, cases are created automatically when an incident is raised from an alert that affects external customers' install base.
    • Assign the CSM event operator role (sn_pro_cs_ops.csm_evt_mgmt_operator on recent versions) to the operators who do this, rather than broad platform roles.
  3. Major issue management. When many customers are affected, use the major issue process. Raise one major case as the parent, and attach child cases for each affected customer, both proactive and customer-raised. Updates on the major case go out to all children, so agents don't type 640 replies.
  4. Communicate first. Send outbound notifications to account contacts from the proactive cases. Show a banner in the customer portal with status and next update time. Contacts who try to open a case see the existing proactive case and can follow it instead.
  5. Enterprise customers. Contacts on accounts with outage-notification entitlements get an immediate notification plus their account manager on copy. Use the account team to identify who.
  6. Noise control. Don't auto-create proactive cases for every alert. Gate the Create Proactive Case rule to alerts that produced an incident, start with manual creation for a month, and review false positives.
  7. Measure. Compare the share of affected customers notified before they raised a case, and the count of customer-raised cases per outage minute. During review, a quick background script shows where the flood came from:
var ga = new GlideAggregate('sn_customerservice_case');
ga.addQuery('opened_at', '>=', gs.hoursAgoStart(2));
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.groupBy('account');
ga.orderByAggregate('COUNT');
ga.query();
while (ga.next()) {
    gs.info(ga.getDisplayValue('account') + ': ' + ga.getAggregate('COUNT'));
}

Trade-offs

  • Automatic proactive cases are fast, but a wrong service map means telling customers about outages they don't have. Start manual, automate once the maps are trusted.
  • One proactive case per customer is clear for reporting, but creates thousands of records in a global outage. The major issue parent keeps agent work manageable.
  • Install base granularity: per tenant is precise but larger to maintain. Per region is simpler but over-notifies.

Common Mistakes

  • Building a custom script that emails all customers when any P1 incident opens. It ignores who is actually affected.
  • Skipping install base and trying to match customers to CIs by name.
  • Leaving customer-raised cases unlinked, so they breach SLAs separately after the outage is fixed.
Score points: Close the loop after the outage. Resolve child cases from the major case with a consistent resolution note, and feed the timeline into the problem record so support and engineering share one post-incident review.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do you handle SLAs on child cases during a declared major issue?
  • How would you notify customers of planned maintenance using the same install base?
  • What would you show on an executive status page during the outage?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: Proactive Customer Service Operations
  • ServiceNow Docs: Create a proactive case from an alert
  • ServiceNow Docs: Customer Service Management and CSDM tables

question: A national retailer with 45,000 employees hires around 8,000 seasonal store associates every October. Onboarding runs on HR lifecycle events, triggered from new HR profile records loaded by a nightly integration from the HR system of record. During last year's peak, HR found: (1) about 6% of new hires got two onboarding cases, (2) remote head-office hires were assigned 'collect your store locker key' tasks, and (3) store managers complained that 30 to 40 tasks arrived on day one with no sequencing. Question: diagnose the likely causes and redesign the onboarding lifecycle event before this year's peak.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Specific knowledge of how lifecycle events are triggered and staged (activity sets, triggers, audiences), awareness of the OOTB trigger flows and their duplicate-case warning, and a sensible design for volume and sequencing. The candidate should prefer configuration over custom scripts.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • How are onboarding cases created today: OOTB trigger flow, a custom business rule, a transform script, or a mix?
  • Does the integration ever re-send or update the same worker, for example a rehire or a start date change?
  • Which data reliably tells us remote versus store: location, job profile, or employee type?
  • Do managers use Employee Center or Journey designer to see their team's tasks?

Diagnosis

  1. Duplicate cases. Human Resources: Core ships trigger flows that create lifecycle event cases from HR profile and job changes. The onboarding one fires when the start date is today or later. These flows are inactive by default, and the docs warn that if more than one is active for the same lifecycle event, duplicates are likely. Six percent duplication is a classic sign of two creators: the OOTB flow plus a legacy business rule or transform script, or a flow that fires on both insert and the update when the integration corrects the start date. Check every flow and business rule that creates sn_hr_le_case records.
  2. Wrong tasks for remote hires. Activities inside an activity set can be limited to an audience. If an activity has no audience, it applies to all employees. The locker-key activity has no audience, or its HR criteria reads a field that the integration leaves empty for head-office staff.
  3. Day-one flood. All activities are probably in one activity set triggered on case creation. Activity sets are meant to model stages, and each one has a trigger: on case creation, after another set completes, or on a condition such as a number of days relative to start date.

Redesign

  • One creator only. Turn on the single OOTB trigger flow for onboarding, or a copy of it if you must change conditions. Retire the other paths. Add a guard that checks for an open onboarding case for the same subject person and HR service. A rehire with a closed case can get a new one; an open case blocks a second.
  • Integration hygiene. Make the import idempotent with a coalesce on the worker ID. Make sure a start-date change updates the existing case rather than creating one.
  • Stage the work. Example sets: Pre-start (triggered on case creation: IT account, uniform order), Day one (triggered by date relative to start: badge, store tour), Week one (after Day one completes: training modules, payroll confirmation), and a 30-day check-in.
  • Audiences via HR criteria. Build "Store-based" and "Remote head office" HR criteria from a field the integration reliably populates. Attach them to activities. Test with real profiles from last year's peak.
  • Manager experience. If Journey designer is licensed, managers see one journey per hire with tasks slotted into stages rather than a flat to-do list.
  • Peak volume. 8,000 cases over a few weeks, each with 20 to 30 tasks, is fine for the platform. The risk is integration batches creating thousands of cases in one run with flows running synchronously. Run the trigger flows in the background, stagger import batches, and load-test a sub-production clone with last year's file.

Trade-offs

  • OOTB trigger flows are upgrade-safe but less flexible. A custom trigger gives control but you own the duplicate logic forever.
  • More activity sets give better sequencing but more configuration for HR admins to maintain. Keep to four or five stages.
  • Strict audiences reduce noise but depend on data quality. Give one fallback activity to HR operations for profiles missing the key field.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding a client or business rule to delete duplicate cases after they are created, instead of fixing the trigger.
  • Writing audience logic as script conditions inside each activity rather than reusable HR criteria.
  • Testing with five hand-made users instead of a full replay of last season's import file.
Score points: Mention the hr_ActivitySet scoped API, for example createLECaseByService, as the supported way to create lifecycle cases in code if a custom trigger is unavoidable. That beats inserting sn_hr_le_case rows directly.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a hire whose start date moves back by two weeks after Pre-start tasks are done?
  • How would you design offboarding for the same seasonal workers in January?
  • What would you put on a dashboard for the HR operations lead during peak?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: HR flows and triggers
  • ServiceNow Docs: Configure the supporting components for a lifecycle event
  • ServiceNow Docs: hr_ActivitySet - Scoped API

question: A manufacturer with plants in Germany, Mexico and the US runs one HRSD instance. The Payroll COE has three country payroll groups plus a global shared-services group of 25 people. Works council rules in Germany say only the German payroll team may see German payroll cases. In UAT, (a) the German payroll lead can't open a case assigned to her own group, (b) a shared-services agent in Mexico can read German payroll cases, and (c) a custom Employee Center widget built by the portal team throws a scope access error when it reads HR cases. Question: diagnose each issue and design the access model.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That the candidate knows HR case access is layered: HR roles, then COE security policies, then cross-scope controls. The candidate should debug each symptom against the right layer, and should not reach for custom ACLs or for granting sn_hr_core.admin.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Is there an existing COE security policy on sn_hr_core_case_payroll, and is it scoped by HR service or by condition?
  • Which field reliably identifies a German case: the subject person's HR profile country, legal entity, or the HR service?
  • What does the shared-services team actually need: create and route only, or read everything?
  • Which scope does the custom widget live in, and does it query HR tables directly?

Diagnosis

  1. (a) Lead can't open her group's case. COE security policies decide which groups can read or write HR cases after creation. A group not listed in a policy can't access those cases, even if its members have sn_hr_core.case_reader. Check that the German payroll group is on the policy covering that service, with write access. Also confirm the lead actually holds a case reader or writer role.
  2. (b) Mexico agent reads German cases. Usually either the shared-services group is listed on a broad payroll policy that covers all services, or the agent holds a role that bypasses COE policies, such as sn_hr_core.admin given "temporarily" during build. Check the agent's effective roles and every policy on the payroll table.
  3. (c) Widget scope error. HR case and HR profile tables use restricted caller access. A widget in another scope reading sn_hr_core_case triggers a cross-scope request that must be approved. Reviewing the restricted caller access record, plus the matching cross-scope privilege, is the documented path. The better question is whether the widget should exist at all. The OOTB Employee Center request widgets already show employees their own HR cases with the correct filtering.

Access Model

  • Policies on sn_hr_core_case_payroll:
    • Germany policy: condition on the case so it matches German subject people. German payroll group gets read and write. No other groups.
    • Mexico and US policies: each country group gets read and write. Shared services gets write, because they triage and route.
    • Keep the conditions simple and indexed. The docs warn that policy conditions can affect performance.
  • Shared-services triage for Germany: let them create and transfer German payroll cases, but not read them after hand-off. COE policies don't control creation, so this works without exceptions.
  • Roles: nobody outside the HR platform owner holds sn_hr_core.admin. Remove it from admin. Turn on the impersonation ACL property so UAT testers can't see data through impersonation.
  • Widget: replace it with OOTB Employee Center components where possible. If it must remain, move it into the HR scope or approve only the specific read access it needs. Never blanket-approve cross-scope access to HR tables.

Trade-offs

  • COE policies versus custom ACLs: policies are the supported mechanism and HR admins can maintain them. Custom ACLs give finer control but are opaque to HR and break more easily on upgrade.
  • Condition-based policies are flexible but cost performance on large case volumes. Policies by HR service are cheaper, but would need separate German services, which duplicates the catalog.
  • Restricting shared services after hand-off protects German data but means they can't answer status questions. Give them a status-only report without sensitive fields.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing (a) by giving the lead sn_hr_core.admin.
  • Writing a before-query business rule to hide German cases, which is invisible to HR admins and fragile.
  • Approving every restricted caller access request in the HR scope to make errors go away.
Score points: Bring a test matrix: each persona (DE payroll, MX payroll, shared services, HR admin, system admin, employee) against each case type with expected read and write. Get the works council representative to sign it off.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do you handle a German employee who transfers to the US mid-year with open payroll cases?
  • How would Now Assist case summarisation interact with these restrictions?
  • How would you audit who read a German payroll case last quarter?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: HR COE security policies
  • ServiceNow Docs: HR profile and HR case security
  • ServiceNow Community: Employee Center ScopeAccessNotGrantedException for HR tables
  • ServiceNow Docs: Restricted caller access privilege

question:
A state government agency runs Discovery across 30 subnets with about 12,000 servers and 4,000 network devices. The nightly schedule now takes 20 hours, so it overlaps the next run. Two MID Servers sit in one data centre at 95% CPU, 28% of Windows hosts end in 'credential failure', and roughly 1,500 devices are only ever classified, never fully explored.
Question: How would you diagnose and redesign the Discovery set-up to finish inside an 8-hour window?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A methodical diagnosis using Discovery status, ECC Queue and MID Server data, then a redesign covering MID Server sizing and placement, clusters, IP range assignment, credential hygiene (including credential affinity), schedule splitting, and fixing classification-only devices. Avoid "just add more MIDs" without evidence.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Where are the 30 subnets relative to the MID Servers? Any WAN links or firewalls in between?
  • Is Discovery pattern-based for these classes, and are there custom patterns or probes?
  • Are credentials rotated by a vault, and is there an external credential store integration?
  • Which devices are business critical and need daily refresh versus weekly?

Diagnosis

  1. Discovery status and device history. Break down the 20 hours: how long scanning, classification and exploration take per range. Ranges with large empty spaces waste Shazzam time.
  2. Credential failures. 28% failure means Discovery is trying every Windows credential against every host and waiting for timeouts. Check whether service accounts are locked, expired or lack WMI/remote rights. Every failed attempt costs time.
  3. ECC Queue backlog and MID Server metrics. If output records wait in "ready" or "processing" for long periods, the MIDs are saturated. Check the MID Server's thread usage and the memory set in its wrapper configuration.
  4. Classification-only devices. Usually missing credentials, blocked ports after classification, or no matching pattern. Look at the device's Discovery log for the step where it stopped.

Redesign

  • Fix credentials first. Clean up the credential list, remove dead accounts, give the Windows account the correct rights, and rely on credential affinity so Discovery tries the credential that last worked for a host first. Scope credentials to the MID Servers or applications that need them.
  • Add and place MID Servers. Size each MID properly (CPU, memory). Put MIDs close to the subnets they scan, assign them IP ranges, and use a load-balancing cluster of MIDs with identical capabilities for the large data centre ranges, plus failover where a secondary site exists. Do not put a MID Server in more than one cluster of the same type (it can sit in one load-balancing and one failover cluster at the same time).
  • Split the schedule. One giant schedule hides problems. Create schedules per site or network zone, staggered across the window, and separate network devices (SNMP) from servers. Critical production ranges run nightly; development and user subnets less often.
  • Tighten IP ranges. Replace broad /16 ranges with the subnets that actually have hosts; exclude printer and VoIP ranges if they are not needed.
  • Use behaviours where protocols differ by zone, so Discovery does not try WMI against Linux-only DMZ ranges.
  • Measure after each change: total duration, credential failure rate, and the classified-only count. Change one thing at a time so you know which fix bought which hours, and record a baseline before you start so the improvement is provable to the agency's change board.

Trade-offs

  • More MID Servers improve throughput but add patching and monitoring overhead.
  • Splitting schedules gives control but more objects to maintain; document an owner per schedule.
  • Reducing frequency for non-critical ranges makes some data older; agree staleness thresholds in CMDB Health so nobody is surprised.

Common Mistakes

  • Increasing MID Server thread counts on an under-sized VM, which makes CPU worse.
  • Adding a MID Server in another site without network reach to the target subnets.
  • Ignoring credential failures; they are often the biggest single time cost.
  • Using a fixed MID Server selection on schedules, which removes automatic failover.
Score points: Quote numbers back: if credential failures fall from 28% to under 5% and each failing host was waiting on timeouts, that alone can reclaim several hours before buying any new hardware.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you monitor MID Server health so a failure is noticed before the next schedule?
  • What is the difference between a failover and a load-balancing MID Server cluster?
  • How would you approach discovery of devices in a segregated network that cannot reach the instance at all?

Sources

  • Configure a MID Server cluster - ServiceNow Docs
  • MID Server selection - ServiceNow Docs
  • Configuring MID Servers - ServiceNow Docs
  • Horizontal discovery process flow with probes and sensors - ServiceNow Docs

question:
An online retailer receives 40,000 events and around 6,000 alerts a day from five monitoring tools. During last Black Friday, a single storage array failure produced 900 alerts across 120 hosts and four teams opened 14 separate incidents before anyone realised it was one problem. The NOC lead wants fewer, smarter incidents before the next peak season, which is 10 weeks away.
Question: Design the alert correlation approach in Event Management. Which grouping methods would you use, in what order, and what has to be true in the CMDB for it to work?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Knowledge of the alert grouping types (rule-based, automated/ML, CMDB-based, tag cluster, text, manual and others), how they interact (an alert belongs to one group at a time), the dependency on CI binding and service maps, and a realistic 10-week plan with measurable outcomes.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • What percentage of alerts are bound to a CI today? Are storage, host and service relationships in the CMDB?
  • Are the e-commerce services mapped (Service Mapping, tags or dynamic CI groups)?
  • How much alert history is available for machine-learning grouping?
  • Who owns incident creation rules today, and do the five tools also open incidents themselves?

Approach

  1. Fix the inputs (weeks 1-3). De-duplication and CI binding come first. Measure the CI-bound rate per tool; target above 85%. Fix node naming and event rules that set the CI. Without binding, CMDB-based grouping and service impact cannot work.
  2. Model the dependency (weeks 2-5). The storage-array case needs storage to host relationships in the CMDB. Discovery can relate hosts to storage; verify a sample. Map the top 10 revenue services with Service Mapping or tag-based mapping so alerts roll up to a service.
  3. Grouping, in layers:
    • Rule-based correlation for known, deterministic patterns: for example, a storage array alert as primary and host disk-latency alerts within 15 minutes as secondary, related through the CMDB. Correlation rules are evaluated in priority order and the first match wins, so keep them few and specific.
    • CMDB-based grouping for alerts on related CIs that rules did not catch.
    • Automated (ML) grouping to find recurring co-occurrence patterns from history; review its groups in a pilot before trusting them for incident creation.
    • Tag cluster grouping where the tools send useful tags (for example the same cluster or availability zone).
  4. One incident per group. Change alert management rules so incidents are created on the parent alert of a group (real or virtual), not on every child, and route to the team owning the primary CI or impacted service.
  5. Peak-season rehearsal (weeks 8-10). Replay or simulate a storage failure in a sub-production instance, check that it forms one group and one incident, and run a NOC dry run.

Success Measures

  • Alert-to-incident ratio and percentage of alerts grouped.
  • Number of duplicate incidents per major event (target: 1).
  • Mean time to identify the probable root cause.
  • Percentage of alerts bound to a CI, tracked per monitoring tool, because one badly configured tool can undo the gains from the other four.

Agree these baselines with the NOC lead in week 1. Without a before-and-after number, a quieter console after peak season can be explained away as a quieter season. Also agree a rollback: every correlation rule and grouping change is deployed through an update set or application with a named owner, so a rule that misbehaves during peak can be switched off in minutes without a change freeze debate.

Trade-offs

  • Rule-based correlation is explainable but brittle and needs maintenance as the estate changes.
  • ML grouping finds patterns nobody wrote, but early on it can group unrelated alerts; operators must trust it before it drives incidents.
  • Strong correlation increases the blast radius of a bad rule: one wrong rule can hide a real, separate outage inside a group.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting with ML before CI binding and de-duplication are fixed.
  • Writing dozens of overlapping correlation rules.
  • Letting the five tools keep opening their own incidents in parallel with Event Management.
Score points: Explain that each alert can belong to only one group and that rule-based groups use a real parent alert, while automated, CMDB and tag-based groups create a virtual parent, so incident rules must handle both.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you stop a bad correlation rule from hiding a separate outage?
  • How does service impact (service health) change what the NOC looks at first?
  • What data would you show the NOC lead after the peak to prove the change worked?

Sources

  • Alert grouping types and creation methods - ServiceNow Docs
  • Alert grouping and use cases - ServiceNow Docs
  • Alert correlation rule form - ServiceNow Docs

question: An airline's check-in and boarding-pass system goes down at 05:40 on a Monday across 60 airports. Within 25 minutes the service desk has logged 340 incidents, three different teams are working the problem separately, and the COO hears about it from social media before IT tells her. The airline uses ServiceNow Incident Management, but Major Incident Management is not configured. In the retrospective, the CIO asks you to design how major incidents should work in ServiceNow so this never happens again. Question: What would you configure, what process would you put around it, and what trade-offs would you call out?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A process-first answer backed by the right OOTB components: the Major Incident Management plugin, candidate/proposal flow, major incident manager role, parent/child linking, communication plans, on-call and post-incident review. The senior signal is knowing what to automate and what to keep as human judgement.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • What defines a major incident for the airline? A service list, number of airports, revenue or safety impact?
  • Who is the major incident manager at 05:40? Is there a 24x7 rota?
  • Which audiences need updates (executives, airport ops, customer service, regulators), on which channels, and how often?
  • Does the CMDB know which business services depend on the check-in platform?

Approach

1. Activate and staff. Activate Incident Management - Major Incident Management (com.snc.incident.mim). It brings related plugins such as Incident Communications Management, Incident Updates and Task-Outage relationship. Grant major_incident_manager to a small, named group on a 24x7 rota built in On-Call Scheduling (com.snc.on_call_rotation). That gives the desk one escalation path instead of three teams finding each other.

2. Candidate and promotion flow.

  • Any agent can propose an incident as a major incident, adding a business impact note. The Major incident state becomes Proposed.
  • A major incident manager accepts (promotes) or rejects it. Promotion can turn the incident itself into the major incident or create a new parent with the candidate as a child, depending on configuration.
  • Trigger rules can propose candidates automatically, for example when more than 15 incidents on the same business service arrive within 10 minutes, or when a P1 is logged against a tier-1 service. They are disabled in the base system. Tune them against history first, or they will create noise.

3. Parent/child handling. The 340 incidents become children of the major incident so agents stop working them in isolation. When the parent is resolved, children are resolved with it and callers are told. Agents should search for an open major incident on the affected service before logging new tickets, and Agent Workspace and the portal can display an active outage banner.

4. Major incident workbench. The MIM team runs the incident from the workbench: timeline, affected services, child incidents, tasks and communications in one place.

5. Communication plans. Pre-build communication plan templates per audience. For example: executives every 30 minutes by email; airport duty managers every 15 minutes by SMS (needs the Notify plugin with a Twilio integration); customer service a status page update; a conference bridge for responders. The workbench tracks each communication task with its due time, so the COO hears from IT on a schedule. Updates to stakeholders are logged on the record for the post-incident review.

6. Close the loop. On resolution, require a post-incident review and create a problem record for root cause, with action items tracked as problem tasks. Report MTTR, time to declare the major incident, and communication SLA adherence.

Trade-offs

  • Automatic vs manual declaration. Trigger rules cut time-to-declare, but false positives at 3 am erode trust. Start with auto-propose, keep promotion human.
  • Promote in place vs new parent. Promoting the first incident keeps history simple. A new parent is cleaner when the first caller's ticket is narrow or holds personal data.
  • Comms channels. SMS and voice need a separate Twilio contract and data-protection review. Email-only is cheaper but slow at 05:40.
  • CMDB dependence. Impact on business services is only as good as service mapping. If the CMDB is weak, keep the declaration criteria simple and human-led.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating "major incident" as just Priority 1. Not every P1 needs a war room.
  • Building a custom "MI" checkbox and custom notifications instead of using the plugin.
  • Leaving 340 tickets unlinked, so 340 callers get no update.
  • No owner for communications, so updates are ad hoc.
  • Skipping the problem record, so the same outage recurs.
Score points: Name time to declare and communication cadence as the two KPIs this airline failed on. Mention that trigger rules are off by default, and that Predictive Intelligence for MIM (a separately licensed plugin) can suggest candidates once there is history. Do not put AI ahead of a working process.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you tie the major incident to an outage record and the service status shown on the portal?
  • Two separate major incidents turn out to share a root cause. How do you handle that?
  • How would you test the major incident process before the next real outage?

Sources

  • Activate Incident Management - Major Incident Management (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Create a major incident candidate (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Add communication plan from the major incident workbench (ServiceNow Docs)

question: A global manufacturer with 11 plants runs a single weekly CAB that reviews about 220 normal changes. Meetings run three hours, 70% of items are approved without discussion, and plant OT (shop-floor) changes sometimes collide with production runs. Last quarter two unreviewed changes caused line stoppages costing an estimated $1.2M. The change approvals are currently hard-coded in a legacy workflow with 14 approval branches. Question: Redesign change risk and approval in ServiceNow so CAB focuses on what matters. What do you configure, how do you migrate, and what are the trade-offs?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That risk should drive the route a change takes. The pieces are risk conditions or a risk assessment, change approval policies made of policy inputs, decisions and approval definitions, change models, the CAB workbench for the reduced agenda, and conflict detection with plant schedules. Plus a safe migration off the legacy workflow.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • What made the two failed changes "unreviewed": wrong risk score, an emergency path, or a missed approval?
  • Are plant OT assets (PLCs, HMIs, line servers) in the CMDB with their plant and line?
  • Do plants have production schedules we can import as blackout or maintenance windows?
  • Which approvals are regulatory (for example, validated systems) and therefore non-negotiable?

Approach

1. Fix risk first. Use risk conditions (Change > Administration > Risk Conditions), one record per rule, for objective facts. Examples: CI is in a plant OT class, the business service is tier 1, no backout plan, or a change outside a maintenance window. Add a short risk assessment questionnaire (weighted questions mapped to thresholds) for what only the requester knows. Validate the scoring by back-testing it against last year's failed changes: both line stoppages should have scored High.

2. Replace the 14 branches with a change approval policy. Policy inputs are the change fields (risk, CI class, plant location, type). Decisions are ordered condition rows, each linked to an approval definition. The policy's Execution setting decides whether only the first matching decision (lowest order) applies, or every matching decision applies. For example:

  • Low risk, IT-only CI: technical peer approval only, no CAB.
  • Moderate risk: assignment group manager plus CI owner.
  • Any plant OT CI: plant engineering manager approval, plus CAB if risk is High.
  • High risk or tier-1 service: CAB.

Decisions are data, so the change manager can maintain them without a developer. Where the decision logic grows, it can be authored with decision builder.

3. Change models. Separate models (for example "Normal - IT", "Normal - Plant OT", Standard, Emergency) give each its own state transitions and policy. Move repeatable low-risk changes to standard change templates, which typically takes a large part of that 70% off the agenda.

4. CAB workbench. Create a CAB definition whose agenda filter brings in only changes that require CAB approval. Requesters are notified when their change is on the agenda, and the change manager runs the meeting with timers and records decisions and notes in the tool. Consider a separate weekly plant CAB with OT engineers.

5. Conflicts. Load plant production runs as blackout schedules and agreed downtime as maintenance schedules tied to the plant's CIs, and make conflict detection mandatory before a change can move to Scheduled. This targets the line-stoppage cause directly.

6. Migrate safely. Run the new policy in parallel for 3 to 4 weeks: changes still follow the legacy workflow, while a report compares what the policy would have required. Cut over by change model, starting with IT-only. Leave in-flight changes on the old workflow until they close, and do not edit the legacy workflow mid-flight.

Trade-offs

  • Fewer CAB items vs perceived control. Auditors may push back. Answer with the policy as evidence and with monthly sampling of auto-approved changes.
  • Condition-based vs ML-based risk. ML risk predictions need clean history and licensing, while rules are transparent. Start with rules.
  • One CAB vs plant CABs. Local CABs know the line but fragment governance. Keep the policy global and the agendas local.
  • Mandatory conflict checks can block urgent fixes. Route those through the emergency model with retrospective review.

Common Mistakes

  • Rebuilding the 14 branches in Flow Designer, which moves the mess without fixing it.
  • Letting the requester set risk manually.
  • Ignoring the policy's Execution setting. With "First decision that matches", only the lowest-order matching decision applies, so a plant OT rule placed below a generic rule never fires. With "Run all decisions that match", every matching approval definition applies. If the business needs sequential approvals (manager then CAB), design for that explicitly.
  • Ignoring the OT CMDB gap. Policies are only as good as the CI data.
Score points: Quantify the outcome, for example "target: CAB agenda below 60 items and no change on a plant CI without a conflict check". Mention back-testing risk rules against historic failures before go-live.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle emergency changes made during a line stoppage?
  • A decision matched but no approval was generated. How would you debug it?
  • How would you measure whether the new design reduced change-caused incidents?

Sources

  • Change approval policies (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Change Advisory Board (CAB) workbench (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Change model management (ServiceNow Docs)
  • How to calculate and configure risk factors in change (ServiceNow Community)

question: A SaaS company supports enterprise customers in New York, London and Singapore. Its contract promises a 1-business-hour first response on P2 incidents. The quarterly SLA report shows 41% of P2 response SLAs breached, but agents and customer success managers insist they respond within 30 minutes, and two strategic customers are now asking for service credits. You find one SLA definition on a 09:00 to 17:00 New York schedule, a stop condition of "Assigned to is not empty", and incidents that move between P3 and P2 during triage. Question: Diagnose what is wrong, fix the definitions, and explain how you would correct the historical data that is already in dispute.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A structured diagnosis of the SLA definition (schedule, timezone source, start, pause, stop and reset conditions, retroactive start), use of the SLA timeline to prove each theory, and a controlled repair of historical task SLAs with validation and audit, because money is involved.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • What does the contract define as "first response": first public comment, or acknowledgement by a named engineer?
  • Whose business hours apply: the customer's region or the support hub's?
  • Should time spent as P3 count once the incident becomes P2?
  • Are there multiple active P2 response definitions, for example old ones never retired?

Diagnosis

  1. Pick 20 breached P2s and open the task SLA records (task_sla). Compare business elapsed time with actual elapsed time, and open the SLA timeline to see exactly when the clock started, paused and stopped.
  2. Schedule and timezone. One New York 09:00 to 17:00 schedule means a Singapore ticket logged at 10:00 local time (about 22:00 in New York) waits until the next New York morning, while Singapore agents answer immediately. The definition is measuring the wrong clock, and the report mixes up who breached.
  3. Stop condition. "Assigned to is not empty" measures assignment, not response. If assignment rules or a triage step assign late, the clock runs on after the engineer has already replied. It can also stop early if someone self-assigns without replying. Either way it does not match the contract.
  4. Priority changes. If the start condition is "Priority is 2" with retroactive start on Created, an incident triaged from P3 to P2 after 3 hours attaches an SLA that is already breached. If the contract says the clock starts when the incident becomes P2, retroactive start is wrong here.
  5. Duplicates. Check for a second active definition covering the same incidents.

Fix

  • Create regional definitions, or one definition with Schedule source set to a task field (for example the customer's support schedule) and a Timezone source matched to the contract.
  • Stop condition: a field that represents a real response, for example a "first responded" date/time set by a business rule when the first customer-visible comment is added by an agent. The SLA engine evaluates conditions on the task, so the response must be captured as a task field.
  • Start condition: Priority is 2 and the condition the contract specifies. Decide deliberately on retroactive start, and document it.
  • Pause: decide whether "Awaiting customer" pauses a response SLA. Usually it should not.
  • Retire (deactivate) the old definition rather than deleting it, so history keeps its reference.

Correct History

Changing a definition does not recalculate existing task SLAs. Use Repair SLA, which rebuilds task SLAs from each task's history. It can be run from the Repair SLAs related link on a task, from a list, or by script. The property com.snc.sla.repair.enabled must be true; it is false by default on upgraded instances. Validate first, then repair in batches outside business hours:

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', '2');
gr.addQuery('sys_created_on', '>=', '2026-07-01 00:00:00');
gr.query();

var repair = new SLARepair();
repair.setValidateOnly(true);   // dry run first; set false to repair
repair.setAuditEnabled(true);
repair.setRunWorkflow(false);   // do not resend breach notifications
repair.repairByFilter(gr.getEncodedQuery(), gr.getRecordClassName());

Limits to know: repair uses the current value of dot-walked fields, not their history, so a customer who has since changed region is recalculated with the new schedule. A "first responded" field that did not exist in Q3 must be backfilled from the journal first, or repair cannot honour it. Snapshot the before-and-after breach report and agree it with Finance and Legal before telling customers.

Trade-offs

  • Regional definitions are easy to read but multiply maintenance. A task-field schedule is elegant but depends on clean customer data.
  • Repairing history fixes the report but may also reveal real breaches. Agree in advance that the corrected numbers are binding.

Common Mistakes

  • Editing task_sla values by hand or with a script, which has no audit trail and will not survive repair.
  • Expecting changes to definitions to fix past records.
  • Running repair with workflows on, which emails customers about old breaches.
Score points: Use setValidateOnly before a real repair, mention the dot-walk limitation, and insist that the contract's wording drives each condition. That shows you treat SLAs as legal data, not just a timer.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you add a 50% warning notification only for strategic accounts?
  • When should a priority change reset an SLA instead of cancelling it?
  • How would you expose live SLA status to customers on the portal?

Sources
