Aim for a few hundred HR services, not thousands. Model pilot union matters as Employee Relations with a dedicated restricted group, not a custom table. Keep outsourced payroll in the Payroll COE. Either give provider staff restricted fulfiller access governed by COE security policies, or integrate to their tool and keep the case owned in ServiceNow.

4. Security model for approval. Present it as a matrix: personas against COEs and countries. Use COE security policies with conditions per legal entity where works councils require it, and the impersonation ACL property. Restricted caller access stays on HR tables. Document which fields are visible to whom, including in reporting and AI.

5. Employee Center. One portal for HR and IT content, with HR criteria and user criteria controlling who sees which topics. Crew mostly use mobile between flights, so design for the mobile app first. Migrate knowledge and retire articles that conflict by country.

6. Journeys. Build cabin crew onboarding as a lifecycle event with staged activity sets. Typical stages are pre-hire, training school, line check and probation, with audiences by base and aircraft type. If Journey designer is licensed, let crew base managers personalise tasks within admin-approved templates.

7. AI, after the data and content are trusted. Start with agent-side features that keep a human in control, such as Now Assist case summarisation and resolution notes for HR agents. Then add employee-facing conversational deflection over curated knowledge. Use the sensitive-topic detection to route matters such as harassment or compensation to a live agent or case, never to a generated answer. Give works councils the evaluation results, the list of topics excluded from AI, and a clear statement of which data the AI skills can read.

8. Sequencing (18 months).

  1. Months 0 to 4: governance, data integration, security model approval, taxonomy.
  2. Months 4 to 9: pilot with one region's shared services and ground staff, using core COEs and Employee Center. Retire one legacy tool.
  3. Months 9 to 14: roll out to the remaining regions, bring payroll providers on, and launch cabin crew onboarding journeys.
  4. Months 12 to 18: pilot union and Employee Relations, AI deflection, and retire the remaining tools. Leave a six-month read-only archive.

Trade-offs

  • Same instance as IT gives one front door and shared onboarding, but needs strong separation of duties. A separate HR instance is simpler politically but breaks the single-portal goal.
  • Migrating closed legacy cases: open cases only is cheaper and cleaner. Full history may be required for Employee Relations, so archive the rest searchable outside ServiceNow.
  • Early AI gives fast visible wins but higher approval risk. Starting with agent-side features builds trust first.

Common Mistakes

  • Recreating each legacy tool's categories one-to-one, which produces thousands of services and useless reporting.
  • Custom tables for unions or crew instead of COEs plus security policies.
  • Switching on AI before knowledge is cleaned up per country.
  • Treating works council approval as a final sign-off rather than a design input from month one.
Score points: Define success metrics up front, such as the share of requests handled through Employee Center, time to productivity for new crew, and number of legacy tools retired. Tie each phase to one of them.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a country that bans storing HR case data outside its borders?
  • What is your plan if the outsourced payroll provider refuses to work in ServiceNow?
  • How would you measure whether AI deflection is actually reducing case volume rather than moving it?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Docs: Exploring Now Assist for HRSD
  • ServiceNow Docs: Agentic workflows for Journey designer
  • ServiceNow Docs: HR COE security policies
  • ServiceNow Docs: HR profile and HR case security

question:
A European telco has nine home-grown integrations loading its CMDB: scripted REST imports from SCCM, Intune, AWS and a network inventory tool, plus spreadsheets from field engineers and a custom feed from an in-house 5G core orchestration platform. Several bypass IRE, there are about 60,000 CIs with no clear data source, and the CMDB team spends two days a month fixing integration breakages after upgrades. The CTO wants a supported, upgrade-safe ingestion architecture within two quarters, and also wants the 5G platform's network functions to appear in service maps.
Question: Design the target ingestion architecture and the transition plan. Show how you would handle the source that has no out-of-box connector.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A clear preference for Service Graph Connectors where they exist, IntegrationHub ETL for sources without one, IRE as the single gate into the CMDB, a source and reconciliation model for every attribute, and a realistic plan to cut over without losing data. For the custom 5G source, a correct use of the IRE API and an honest view of when Service Mapping patterns, tags or relationships from the source are appropriate.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Which of the nine sources overlap (for example SCCM and Intune on the same laptops; AWS connector and Cloud Discovery)?
  • Does the 5G orchestration platform expose an API with stable identifiers and the relationships between network functions and hosts?
  • What are the licensing entitlements for ITOM Visibility and Service Graph Connectors?
  • Who will own each integration after go-live?

Target Architecture

  1. Service Graph Connectors from the ServiceNow Store for SCCM, Intune and AWS, and for the network tool if a connector exists. They use IntegrationHub ETL and the Robust Transform Engine for mapping and IRE for writes, and depend on the Integration Commons for CMDB app for shared transforms and the CMDB Integrations Dashboard. They are maintained by ServiceNow or the partner, which addresses the upgrade-breakage problem.
  2. IntegrationHub ETL for spreadsheets and any remaining tabular source without a connector: guided mapping to CMDB classes, Integration Commons transforms for normalisation, IRE underneath.
  3. IRE API for the event-style 5G feed where records arrive individually through a scripted REST endpoint or a flow.
  4. Every source registered as a value in the discovery_source choice list, with reconciliation rules defined per class and attribute, so each attribute has a known owner.

The 5G Source: IRE in a Scoped App

(function () {
    var payload = {
        items: [{
            className: 'cmdb_ci_linux_server',
            internal_id: 'host1',
            values: { name: 'nfvi-host-17', serial_number: 'SN-55120', ip_address: '10.40.2.17' }
        }, {
            className: 'cmdb_ci_appl',
            internal_id: 'nf1',
            values: { name: 'AMF-instance-03', version: '5.2.1' }
        }],
        relations: [{ parent: 1, child: 0, type: 'Runs on::Runs' }]
    };

    var result = sn_cmdb.IdentificationEngine.createOrUpdateCIEnhanced(
        '5G Orchestrator',          // must exist as a discovery_source choice value
        JSON.stringify(payload),
        {}                          // options object is required; empty is allowed
    );

    var out = JSON.parse(result);
    for (var i = 0; i < out.items.length; i++) {
        gs.info(out.items[i].className + ' ' + out.items[i].operation + ' ' + out.items[i].sysId);
    }
})();

During build, run the same payload through the global SNC.IdentificationEngineScriptableApi.identifyCI() (for example from a background script) to see whether it would insert or update without committing; the scoped sn_cmdb.IdentificationEngine API only documents createOrUpdateCI and createOrUpdateCIEnhanced. The application CI is a dependent CI, so it needs the relationship to its host to be identified; sending it alone produces an identification error, which is the correct behaviour. If the network functions deserve their own class, create a custom class with its own identification rule rather than overloading cmdb_ci_appl.

Service Maps for 5G

Pattern-based top-down mapping is precise but needs credentials and patterns for every technology; for a fast-changing virtualised core, tag-based mapping or relationships supplied by the orchestrator (via IRE, as above) are usually more sustainable. Tag-based maps are less precise and do not map component connections, so critical customer-facing paths may still warrant patterns.

Transition Plan

  1. Baseline: classify the 60,000 unknown-source CIs by class and last update; many will be stale and go straight into CMDB Data Manager retirement.
  2. One source at a time: install the connector in sub-production, run against the same data as the legacy integration, compare inserts versus updates, and only then switch off the legacy job. A connector's first run in production should produce mostly updates, not inserts.
  3. Reconciliation before cut-over: rules in place so the new source does not overwrite better data.
  4. Decommission each custom integration and remove its code and scheduled jobs.
  5. Operate: use the CMDB Integrations Dashboard and IRE output for daily monitoring, with an owner per connector.

Trade-offs

  • Connectors are upgrade-safe but opinionated; custom fields from a source may need ETL extensions.
  • IntegrationHub ETL is quicker than code for tabular data but less suited to event-style, single-record feeds, where the IRE API fits better.
  • Dual-running legacy and new integrations is safer but can create duplicates if identification differs; time-box it.

Common Mistakes

  • Writing directly to CMDB tables with GlideRecord in the custom feed, bypassing IRE.
  • Using an unregistered source name, which IRE rejects.
  • Switching on a connector in production without reconciliation rules and watching it overwrite owned attributes.
Score points: Frame the result as one rule: every CI write goes through IRE with a registered source, and every attribute has an owner. That rule is what makes upgrades and audits uneventful.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a connector's class mapping that conflicts with your CSDM model?
  • What would you monitor daily to know an integration has silently stopped?
  • When would you still build a custom pattern rather than rely on an external source?

Sources

  • Integration Commons for CMDB - ServiceNow Docs
  • Service Graph Connector for SolarWinds - ServiceNow Docs
  • IdentificationEngine - Scoped API reference - ServiceNow Docs
  • Map application services using tags with classic Service Mapping - ServiceNow Docs

question: A Tier-1 bank's IT organisation handles about 85,000 incidents a month with 1,200 agents. The CIO has committed to cutting incident volume by 25% and MTTR by 30% in 18 months, and the board wants generative AI to be "part of the answer" while the regulator expects explainability and human oversight. Problem Management exists on paper but has 900 open problems with no root cause, the knowledge base has 14,000 articles of which most are stale, and resolution notes are usually "fixed". Question: As the ITSM architect, design the programme across Problem, Knowledge, Predictive Intelligence and Now Assist. What would you do first, what would you deliberately not do, and how would you govern it?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That AI amplifies the quality of the underlying data and process. The data has to be fixed and measured first, through problem discipline, knowledge hygiene and good resolution notes. AI goes in where it removes toil and is reviewable by a human, with a governance model a regulator would accept. Sequencing and measurement matter more than features.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • What share of the 85,000 is repeat demand (password, access, known application errors) vs genuine new faults?
  • Which entitlements are licensed today (ITSM Pro, Now Assist for ITSM, Process Mining)?
  • What does the bank's model risk management policy require for AI features: inventory, testing, human-in-the-loop?
  • Are agents in Service Operations Workspace or the classic UI?

Approach (phased)

Phase 0, baseline (months 0 to 2). Build Performance Analytics indicators: incidents per service per 1,000 users, repeat-incident rate, reassignment count, MTTR by priority, knowledge use (articles attached to resolved incidents), and problem age. Use Process Mining on incidents to find where tickets ping-pong between groups and where time is lost. Without a baseline, "25%" cannot be shown.

Phase 1, problem discipline (months 1 to 6).

  • Triage the 900 open problems: close those with no recent incidents, and merge duplicates.
  • Run the problem state model properly (New, Assess, Root Cause Analysis, Fix in Progress, Resolved, Closed). Use Accept Risk for problems the bank chooses not to fix, with an owner and an expiry.
  • Identify the top 20 incident clusters by volume using Predictive Intelligence similarity and clustering on short descriptions. Open problems against them with named owners and a fix-funding path through change.
  • Publish known error articles with workarounds (linked through the Primary Known Error article field on the problem's Analysis Information tab), so the desk can resolve repeat contacts at first touch.

Phase 2, knowledge hygiene and capture. Retire or archive articles not viewed in 12 months, assign every knowledge base an owner, and adopt a KCS-style loop: agents search first, link or create an article on resolution, and flag bad articles. Make the resolution code and a meaningful resolution note mandatory for P1 to P3 through form configuration, not trust.

Phase 3, AI where it removes toil.

  • Now Assist for ITSM incident summarisation for handoffs and major incident updates. It draws on description, work notes, comments and resolution notes, and needs enough text to be useful (some releases enforced a minimum word count on the input fields).
  • Resolution notes generation at resolve time. This directly fixes the "fixed" problem and feeds better data to knowledge and problem work. Configure the trigger (automatic or user-initiated) in the Now Assist Admin console, and require agents to review before saving.
  • Predictive Intelligence assignment as a recommendation, then automatic for high-precision groups.
  • Generating knowledge articles from resolved incidents, with a mandatory human review state before publishing.

Pilot with 2 to 3 groups. Restrict access with a dedicated role or group rather than all itil users, A/B measure against control groups, then expand.

What I Would Not Do

  • Let generated content publish to customers or close tickets without human review.
  • Turn on every skill for 1,200 agents on day one.
  • Train ML models on the current mis-routed history without cleansing it.
  • Promise the 25% from AI alone. Most volume reduction comes from fixing problems and deflecting repeat demand through self-service and Virtual Agent with good knowledge.

Governance

  • An AI feature inventory: what each skill uses as input, who can use it, its trigger mode, and its owner.
  • Human-in-the-loop points recorded on the task (agent accepted or edited the summary or notes).
  • Quality sampling: a monthly review of generated resolution notes and articles against a rubric.
  • Data residency and privacy review of which fields are sent to the model, with redaction of customer account data where required.
  • A monthly steering group reviewing the KPIs, with authority to switch a skill off.

Trade-offs

  • Speed vs evidence. A pilot with control groups delays the board story by a quarter but produces numbers the regulator and the CFO will accept.
  • Automatic vs manual AI triggers. Automatic gets more adoption but more unreviewed output. Manual is safer but adoption lags.
  • Central problem team vs embedded problem owners. A central team keeps rigour, while embedded owners give fixes a home in delivery teams. A hybrid is usual.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting with a chatbot on top of 14,000 stale articles.
  • Measuring AI by usage counts instead of MTTR and repeat-incident rate.
  • Treating problem management as a report rather than funded engineering work.
Score points: Show the dependency chain: better resolution notes lead to better knowledge and similarity clustering, which lead to better problems and fixes, which lead to lower volume. Also note that Now Assist resolution notes generation is valuable mainly because it repairs the data that every later step depends on.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you prove to auditors that a human reviewed AI-generated resolution notes?
  • Six months in, volume is down 8%. What do you look at?
  • How would you prioritise which problems get engineering funding?

Sources

  • Now Assist for IT Service Management (ITSM) (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Generate the resolution notes for an incident using Now Assist for ITSM (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Investigate root cause of a problem (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Process Mining for Problem Management: incident patterns (ServiceNow Community)

question: A global logistics company is consolidating 40 point-to-point integrations into ServiceNow: hand-written SOAP and REST scripts, a nightly 3-million-row shipment master file, on-prem warehouse systems, and SaaS tools (HR, identity, collaboration). The enterprise already runs Apache Kafka as its event backbone and publishes about 2 million shipment status events a day. The operations VP wants ServiceNow to open exceptions (lost or delayed high-value shipments) within two minutes of the event. Integration failures today are discovered by users, not by IT. Question: Design the target integration architecture: which ServiceNow integration pattern for which flow, how you handle volume and performance, and how you govern and operate 40 integrations.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A pattern-based architecture rather than one tool for everything: event streaming for high-volume events with filtering upstream, bulk import for master data, IntegrationHub spokes for SaaS, MID Servers for on-prem, plus credential management, platform protection limits, and an operating model with monitoring and ownership.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Of 2 million events a day, how many are real exceptions that need a ServiceNow record?
  • Is the Stream Connect subscription (and the Workflow Data Fabric subscription it depends on) affordable, or is Kafka-to-REST via middleware the fallback?
  • Does the shipment master file need to be in ServiceNow at all, or only the subset referenced by exceptions?
  • Who owns each source system and its interface contract?

Approach: pattern per flow

  • Shipment events (Kafka): Do not stream 2 million events a day into task tables. Filter and enrich upstream (a stream-processing rule raises only exception events to a dedicated topic). Consume that topic with Stream Connect for Apache Kafka, which connects through the Hermes Messaging Service and offers a Kafka Message trigger for flows plus ETL, transform map and script consumers. A flow creates or updates the exception case, using the shipment ID as the correlation key so repeat events update rather than duplicate. This meets the two-minute target without polling.
  • Outbound events (exception resolved) go back to Kafka with the Kafka Producer step or the ProducerV2 API, so downstream systems subscribe rather than being called one by one.
  • Shipment master file (3 million rows): question whether it is needed; if yes, load deltas only, through a scheduled data import with a coalesce on an indexed key. Use concurrent imports (multiple import sets transformed in parallel) only after indexes and transform scripts are tuned, and only if row order does not matter. Run it in an agreed batch window.
  • SaaS (HR, identity, collaboration): IntegrationHub spokes first; custom spokes built with the spoke generator or REST step where none exists. Connection and credential aliases so each instance has its own endpoints.
  • On-prem warehouse systems: MID Server clusters per region, JDBC or REST through the MID; mTLS where required, checked against the release's supported options.
  • Legacy SOAP scripts: retire into flows and spokes, or into a Scripted REST facade where a partner can only push.

Volume and performance protection

  • Inbound REST rate limit rules per integration user; require callers to honour 429 with backoff.
  • Keep integration pool headroom for MID Server traffic; avoid synchronous outbound calls inside user transactions.
  • Async processing for anything not needed within the user's save.
  • Load-test the event path and the import in a production-sized sub-prod instance before go-live.

Governance and operations

  • Integration catalogue: each of the 40 integrations recorded with owner, pattern, data classification, volume, SLA and credential alias; new integrations go through the design authority.
  • Standards: dedicated integration users with least privilege, no credentials in scripts, correlation IDs, retries with backoff, idempotency, versioned APIs.
  • Observability: every integration writes success and failure metrics; failures create tasks for an integration support group; dashboards on error rate, latency, Kafka undelivered and unprocessed messages, and ECC queue backlog. IT should find failures before users do.
  • Lifecycle: ATF and contract tests in the pipeline; integrations included in clone profiles so sub-prod never calls production endpoints.

Trade-offs

  • Stream Connect versus middleware (MuleSoft, Boomi or custom consumers posting REST): native is lower latency and fewer hops but adds subscription cost and platform-specific skills; middleware centralises enterprise integration but adds latency and another team in the critical path.
  • Replicating master data simplifies reporting but adds load and staleness; looking it up on demand keeps one source of truth but couples ServiceNow to source availability.
  • Instance Data Replication is the right tool only for ServiceNow-to-ServiceNow table replication, not for external systems.

Common Mistakes

  • Turning ServiceNow into the event store for every shipment status.
  • One shared integration user for all 40 integrations, making rate limits and audit useless.
  • No owner per integration, so failures sit in logs nobody reads.
  • Reaching for concurrent imports before fixing a missing coalesce index.
Score points: Start with a "filter at the edge" principle and quantify it: if only 0.5 percent of events are exceptions, ServiceNow processes about 10,000 events a day instead of 2 million, which changes the whole sizing discussion.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a Kafka consumer outage of two hours without losing exceptions?
  • How would you migrate the 40 integrations without a big-bang cutover?
  • Where would you enforce data classification for shipment and customer data?

Sources

  • Using Stream Connect for Apache Kafka (ServiceNow docs)
  • Stream Connect quick start guide (ServiceNow docs)
  • Concurrent imports (ServiceNow docs)
  • Exploring Instance Data Replication (ServiceNow docs)

question: A global pharmaceutical company has 14 delivery teams (internal and two partners) building on one production instance: ITSM, HR Service Delivery, a GxP-validated quality-event app and several scoped apps. Today they use one shared dev instance, update sets, manual promotion every two weeks and spreadsheets for test evidence. Releases slip, auditors question validation evidence, and the last two upgrades took four months each. The CIO wants a delivery model that supports weekly releases for low-risk apps, validated releases for GxP apps, and upgrades twice a year. Question: Design the instance strategy, source control and CI/CD approach, testing gates and the governance (Center of Excellence) needed to make this work.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

An architecture that matches change type to delivery mechanism, a realistic instance landscape, a pipeline built on the platform's CI/CD API and ATF, automated quality gates (Instance Scan), audit-ready evidence for GxP, and a governance body with real decision rights, not just tooling.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • How many instances are licensed today and is budget available for more?
  • Which work is global-scope customization of OOTB apps versus scoped custom apps?
  • What does the quality unit accept as validation evidence (computer software assurance approach, risk-based testing)?
  • Which CI tool is the enterprise standard (GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, Jenkins, GitLab)?

Approach

1. Classify changes by delivery mechanism.

  • Scoped custom apps (including the GxP app): Git source control linked from Studio, branches per feature, applications published to the company application repository and installed downstream by version.
  • Configuration of OOTB global apps (ITSM, HRSD): update sets remain the practical mechanism, but grouped into update set batches per release, with naming and ownership rules.
  • Data and admin changes (groups, assignment rules) go through a standard change process, not code pipelines.

2. Instance landscape. A typical target: one or more dev instances (a separate dev for the GxP stream to keep validated work isolated), test, a validation/UAT instance controlled by quality, a staging/pre-prod refreshed from production for upgrades and performance tests, and production. Personal sandboxes for partners where licensing allows. A clone calendar keeps test and staging fresh, with a standard clone profile (preserve integration endpoints and credentials, exclude bulky logs, mask personal data).

3. Pipeline using the CI/CD API. ServiceNow exposes REST endpoints under /api/sn_cicd/ (role sn_cicd.sys_ci_automation) to apply source control changes, publish to and install from the app repository, roll back an install, run an ATF test suite and run instance scans; calls are asynchronous and return a progress ID you poll. ServiceNow publishes sample GitHub workflows and actions, and a Jenkins plugin, built on these endpoints.

  • On pull request: apply branch changes to a dev or CI instance, run an Instance Scan point or suite scan on the app, run the app's ATF suite; fail the PR on new high findings or failed tests.
  • On merge: publish a new app version to the repository, install on test, run regression ATF, install on validation.
  • Release: a change request (standard change for low-risk apps; normal change with quality approval for GxP), then install to production with the rollback endpoint as the back-out plan.

4. Validation evidence. ATF results, scan results, approvals and the deployed version are generated by the pipeline and stored with the change record, giving auditors traceable, repeatable evidence instead of spreadsheets. Apply risk-based testing: deep scripted testing for GxP-relevant functions, lighter regression for the rest.

5. Upgrade cadence. The same ATF suites become the upgrade regression pack; upgrade staging first, review skipped records with a strict revert-by-default policy, and track customization of OOTB records as a CoE metric.

6. Center of Excellence. Platform owner, architects forming a design authority (approves new scoped apps, OOTB customizations, integrations), a release manager owning the calendar, a CoE-owned coding standard enforced by Instance Scan checks, a demand board, partner onboarding standards, and a technical debt budget each release. Metrics: lead time, change failure rate, ATF coverage of critical journeys, open high findings, upgrade duration.

Trade-offs

  • More instances increase cost and clone effort but give isolation the GxP stream needs.
  • Source control works well for scoped apps; global-scope ITSM tweaks do not branch and merge cleanly, so forcing everything into Git creates friction.
  • Weekly releases demand automated tests; without ATF coverage the pipeline only automates risk.
  • Pro-code options such as the ServiceNow SDK with Fluent bring standard Git and CI workflows for some teams, but add skill requirements.

Common Mistakes

  • Buying a pipeline tool before agreeing ownership and a definition of done.
  • Allowing partners to customize OOTB records without design authority review.
  • Treating ATF as a one-off project instead of a maintained asset.
  • Letting the validation instance drift from production configuration.
Score points: Sequence the rollout: start with one scoped app and its ATF suite as a lighthouse, measure lead time and failure rate, then onboard teams in waves; a big-bang switch across 14 teams usually fails.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do you handle a hotfix that must skip the weekly cadence?
  • How do you stop two teams changing the same global business rule in different update sets?
  • What would convince the quality unit that automated evidence is sufficient?

Sources

  • Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CICD) API (ServiceNow docs)
  • ServiceNow/sncicd_githubworkflow sample workflows (GitHub)
  • ServiceNow CI/CD Jenkins pipeline steps
  • Clone Admin Console (ServiceNow docs)

question: A managed service provider runs one ServiceNow instance for 45 customers: hospitals, two state government agencies and a defence supplier. A new government contract requires that the agency's ticket data is not visible to other tenants, that sensitive fields are encrypted with keys the agency controls, and that no real personal data exists in development and test. The defence supplier has asked whether it can stay on the shared instance at all. The MSP's head of platform asks you for a target architecture. Question: What do you recommend for tenancy, encryption and non-production data, and where would you tell a customer that the shared instance is the wrong answer?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A clear view of what domain separation does and does not isolate, a correct comparison of the encryption options, privacy controls for clones, and the judgement to recommend a separate instance where the requirement exceeds what logical separation can guarantee.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Is the instance already domain separated, and how many domain levels exist?
  • Does the contract say "not visible" (logical separation) or "not co-located" (physical separation)?
  • Which fields are sensitive, and must they be searchable or reportable?
  • Who must hold the keys, and must the MSP be technically unable to read the data?
  • How are non-production instances refreshed today?

Approach

1. Tenancy with domain separation. Each record carries one domain in its sys_domain field, and related records inherit the parent's domain by default. Follow the documented hierarchy: TOP holds the MSP's processes and overrides and never contains users; a default domain catches orphaned data and is visible only to the provider; each customer gets its own domain under the hierarchy, with restricted and unrestricted customer branches. Do not domain-separate platform tables with the sys_ prefix. Avoid moving data between domains while the instance is in use. Test every customer-facing process with users of different domains, because not every application and feature is equally domain aware.

2. Know the limit. ServiceNow's own guidance is that complete isolation of everything, including system properties, is not achievable within one instance; total separation needs separate instances. Admins at the MSP still operate the whole platform, and shared configuration changes affect all tenants.

3. Encryption options.

  • Column Level Encryption (included): field-level encryption with ServiceNow-managed keys only, and a limit of five encryption modules and five module access policies.
  • Column Level Encryption Enterprise (subscription): built on the Key Management Framework, supports customer-supplied keys, automatic key rotation and module access policies that limit decryption to specific users, scripts or application scopes. This is the option for "fields encrypted with keys the agency controls". Note that recent documentation flags both column-level products for future deprecation in favour of Field Encryption and Field Encryption Enterprise, so plan for that path.
  • Cloud Encryption: database-level AES-256 encryption at rest, with ServiceNow-generated or customer-supplied keys. It protects the storage layer but does not hide data from users who have access through the application.

Encrypted fields have functional costs: limited searching, sorting and reporting. Encrypt the few fields that need it and use ACLs, including query ACLs, for the rest.

4. Non-production data. Use Data Privacy clone de-identification policies so anonymization runs on the target during the clone and the target never holds the original sensitive values. Know its limits: it works on properly classified structured data; journal fields, attachments and logs are not anonymized, so exclude or purge them through clone exclusions, and remember that SSO can resynchronize user data after the clone. Data privacy cloning is not available for self-hosted instances.

5. Recommendation by customer.

  • Hospitals: shared instance, domain separated, with encryption for selected clinical fields and anonymized clones.
  • State agencies: shared instance is defensible only if the contract accepts logical separation; add enterprise-tier field encryption with agency-held keys and module access policies. If the contract requires physical separation or a specific government cloud, recommend a dedicated instance.
  • Defence supplier: recommend a dedicated instance, likely in a regulated hosting offering. Its requirements usually include data residency, personnel screening and isolation that domain separation cannot provide.

Trade-offs

  • Shared instance: lower cost and one upgrade, but every change is a 45-customer change and isolation is logical only.
  • Dedicated instances: strongest isolation and independent upgrade windows, but more instances to run, and cross-customer reporting needs a separate data pipeline.
  • Customer-held keys: stronger assurance, but key loss or revocation makes data unreadable, so key custody and recovery procedures must be in the contract.

Common Mistakes

  • Selling domain separation as "physical isolation".
  • Assuming Cloud Encryption satisfies a requirement that the MSP's own admins cannot read the data.
  • Encrypting dozens of fields and breaking reporting and search.
  • Cloning production into test before Data Privacy policies are in place.
Score points: Turn each requirement into the control that satisfies it and the evidence for auditors: domain assignment tests, key custody records, module access policy reviews and clone anonymization logs. And be willing to say "this customer needs its own instance".

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do you handle a shared knowledge base or catalog that some tenants should see and others not?
  • What happens to encrypted data if the agency revokes its key?
  • How would you migrate one tenant out to a dedicated instance later?

Sources

  • Domain separation hierarchies
  • Encryption (platform security)
  • Column Level Encryption Enterprise
  • Data privacy clone

question: A European telco (28,000 employees, 3 SOC shifts, an MSSP covering nights) runs ServiceNow ITSM today. Security handles incidents in a separate ticketing tool fed by the SIEM, tracks vulnerabilities in spreadsheets exported from Tenable and Rapid7, and the regulator now expects documented, timely handling of security incidents and proof that critical exposures are fixed. The CISO wants Security Incident Response and Vulnerability Response on the existing ITSM instance within a year. The ITSM team worries about security data leaking to 6,000 fulfiller users; the SOC worries about alert floods and slow manual triage. Question: As the architect, how do you design and sequence this rollout, and what are the decisions you would put in front of the CISO?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A phased plan that ties both products to the CMDB and to the existing ITSM processes, protects security data with the product's role model rather than custom hacks, controls alert volume before automating, and gives the CISO measurable outcomes for the regulator.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • What volume of SIEM alerts per day, and what share become real incidents today?
  • How good is the CMDB for servers and network gear? Both products depend on it for ownership and business impact.
  • What must the MSSP be able to see and do, and under what contract terms?
  • Which regulator deadlines apply (initial notification windows, reporting format)?
  • Are there threat intelligence feeds or a SOAR tool already in place?

Approach

Phase 0: Foundations (first 8 weeks). CMDB coverage and ownership for servers, network devices and business services; group structure for SOC tiers, MSSP and resolver teams; a data classification decision for security records.

Phase 1: Security Incident Response.

  • Ingest from the SIEM as security incidents, but filter and correlate in the SIEM first. Only alerts that meet an agreed fidelity bar should create incidents; the rest stay as events in the SIEM. Automating triage on a flood just makes the flood faster.
  • Use the base severity calculators to derive severity from business impact and affected CIs, and tune them with the SOC rather than writing custom scoring.
  • Use the base playbooks, built on Flow Designer, as the starting point. Copy a base playbook and adjust it; do not edit base content. Start with two or three high-volume patterns (phishing, malware on endpoint, suspicious login) and automate enrichment steps first, containment second, after the SOC trusts the outputs.
  • Map incidents to MITRE ATT&CK tactics so post-incident reporting speaks the regulator's and the SOC's language.
  • Security incidents spawn tasks to IT resolver groups. Those tasks should expose only what the resolver needs; the parent security incident stays restricted.

Phase 2: Vulnerability Response. Bring in Tenable and Rapid7 through their integrations, fix CI matching before go-live, configure remediation target rules aligned to the telco's patch policy, and group findings into remediation tasks by vulnerability and assignment group. Route patching through Change where the telco's change policy requires it. Use exception (deferral) workflows with two-level approval for systems that cannot be patched, so risk acceptance is recorded rather than implied.

Phase 3: Connect them. Show open critical exposures on the affected CI inside a security incident, and use incident learnings to raise priority on related vulnerabilities.

Protecting the data. Rely on the SIR and VR roles: sn_si.analyst is the base role for security incident work and sn_si.admin has full control, so fulfiller users without these roles cannot read security incidents. Keep the base ACLs, add restrictions rather than loosening them, test with impersonation of an ordinary ITIL user, and review the result with internal audit. For the MSSP, use a dedicated group with only the analyst role and, if the contract requires it, conditions that limit them to the incident types they handle. Do not make a copy of ITSM tables to hide data; that creates two sources of truth.

Decisions for the CISO

  • Same instance versus a separate security instance. Same instance gives shared CMDB, change and resolver groups, which is why most customers choose it; a separate instance gives stronger isolation but duplicates the CMDB and complicates task hand-offs.
  • Which alert sources create incidents automatically, and who owns the fidelity threshold.
  • How far playbooks may act without a human (enrichment only, or also containment such as disabling accounts).
  • Risk acceptance authority for deferred vulnerabilities.

Trade-offs

  • Speed versus trust: automating containment early saves minutes but one bad automated action can take down a customer-facing service in a telco.
  • Strict data segregation reduces leakage but slows collaboration with IT; restricted parent records with shareable child tasks balance both.
  • Going live with VR before CMDB quality is acceptable gives quick numbers but misrouted work, which destroys trust with resolver teams.

Common Mistakes

  • Sending every SIEM alert into ServiceNow.
  • Customizing base playbooks directly, then struggling with upgrades.
  • Granting the analyst role broadly "so IT can help", which defeats the segregation.
  • Launching SIR and VR in the same quarter with the same small team.
Score points: Give the CISO metrics that map to the regulator: mean time to detect and contain by severity, percentage of incidents with documented timeline, percentage of critical vulnerabilities fixed within target, and the number and age of accepted risks.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you share indicators of compromise with peer telcos from a security incident?
  • What would you change if the regulator required a 24-hour initial notification?
  • Where would AI-assisted triage or summarization help, and what guardrails would you set?

Sources

  • Components installed with Security Incident Response (roles)
  • Calculate the severity of a security incident
  • Security Incident Response playbook resources
  • Request an extension for a Vulnerability Response exception rule

question: A state government department with 22,000 employees across 9 agencies runs three self-service experiences: an IT Service Portal (/sp) with 640 catalog items, an HR portal, and a SharePoint intranet with 2,000 policy pages. Employees do not know where to go, 18% of IT requests are raised against the wrong item, and each agency insists on its own branding and categories. Leadership wants one front door within 12 months, with privacy rules preventing some agencies from seeing others' HR content. Question: As the platform architect, how would you plan the consolidation onto Employee Center, covering taxonomy, catalog rationalisation, access, migration and governance?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

That this is an information architecture and governance programme, not a theme change. Expect: a unified taxonomy built around employee intent, catalog rationalisation before migration, user criteria for agency and privacy boundaries, a redirect plan (URL suffix, page route maps), measurable adoption, and a content operating model.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • Are all nine agencies on one instance and one HR data model, or are some on separate instances?
  • What exactly do the privacy rules restrict: HR policies, HR cases, or both?
  • Which agency branding is a legal requirement and which is preference?
  • Will SharePoint stay as the source for policies (linked) or be migrated into ServiceNow knowledge?

Approach

1. Rationalise before you migrate. 640 items with an 18% wrong-item rate means duplicates and jargon. Pull 12 months of request volume per item. Retire anything with near-zero use, merge near-duplicates into one item with variables (for example, one "Software request" item instead of 120 per-product items), and rename items in employee language. A realistic target is 30 to 50% fewer items. Order guides cover bundles such as onboarding.

2. One taxonomy, built around intent. The Employee Center unified taxonomy is a hierarchy of topics that brings together catalog items, knowledge, quick links and other content types across departments. Design it with card sorting and search logs, using topics like "Pay and benefits", "My laptop and phone" and "Travel", not around the org chart. Start from a copy of the default taxonomy. Agencies get sub-topics and banner images, not separate portals. Remember that topic-to-content associations are data: they do not travel in update sets, so plan to move them as XML or data loads.

3. Access and privacy. Use user criteria on catalog items and knowledge bases, built from agency and department data on sys_user, so an employee of Agency A never sees Agency B's HR policies. Not Available For overrides Available For, which is useful for contractors. User criteria control catalog visibility, not data, so HR case data stays protected by HR Service Delivery's own security model and ACLs. Test with personas from each agency, and run a privacy sign-off.

4. External content. Use quick links to point to SharePoint policies in phase 1, so the taxonomy is complete on day one. Migrate only high-traffic policies into knowledge, where feedback and search analytics work.

5. Cutover. Follow the documented migration path:

  • Install Employee Center.
  • Build the taxonomy, with banner and thumbnail images per topic.
  • Add every request type to My Request filters so IT and HR requests appear together.
  • Configure to-dos to include approvals.
  • Change the old portal's URL suffix, and use page route maps to redirect old /sp pages to their Employee Center equivalents so bookmarks and emailed links keep working.
  • Install Service Portal Analytics for the new portal.

Pilot with one or two agencies (Employee Center supports starting with a single department and adding more later). Then onboard agencies in waves of three.

6. Governance. Create a content council with one taxonomy owner (central) and agency content managers who can add items within their topics but cannot create new top-level topics. Rules: every new catalog item needs an owner, a review date and a taxonomy placement. Quarterly, retire items with no requests in 6 months. Measure wrong-item rate (reclassified RITMs), search-with-no-click rate, portal deflection and CSAT per agency.

Trade-offs

  • Single taxonomy vs agency autonomy. Too much central control and agencies build shadow portals. Too little and the taxonomy fragments again. Branding via topic imagery is the usual compromise.
  • Link vs migrate SharePoint. Linking is fast but splits search and analytics. Migrating is better long-term but is a content project in its own right.
  • Big bang vs waves. Waves reduce risk but mean two front doors for months. Mitigate with redirects and messaging.
  • Customising widgets. Heavy widget cloning blocks upgrades. Prefer configuration, and theme only where the brand requires it.

Common Mistakes

  • Lifting and shifting 640 items and their categories into topics one to one.
  • Using user criteria as the only HR privacy control.
  • Forgetting redirects, so thousands of old links break on day one.
  • Moving taxonomy content links through update sets and finding the topics empty in production.
  • No owner per item after go-live.
Score points: Tie success to numbers: wrong-item rate from 18% to under 5%, catalog down by a third, and a single entry URL with redirects. Also mention that the taxonomy is an ongoing product with an owner, not a one-off build.

Likely Follow-ups

  • One agency is on a separate instance. How do you include it in the front door?
  • How would you design search so that "pay slip" finds both the HR article and the request item?
  • How would you make the portal accessible (WCAG) for a government audience?

Sources

  • Migrate to Employee Center from Service Portal (ServiceNow Docs)
  • Unified Taxonomy for Employee Center (ServiceNow Docs)
  • FAQs on Employee Center adoption and deployment (ServiceNow Community)
  • Apply user criteria to items and categories (ServiceNow Docs)

question: What is the ServiceNow SDK (Now SDK) and Fluent, and when would you use it instead of App Engine Studio?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

They want to know you understand the modern, code-first way to build ServiceNow apps — the Now SDK and its declarative Fluent library — and that you can articulate when it beats clicking through App Engine Studio. Strong candidates frame it as source-control-first development, not a replacement for the platform.

The Answer

The ServiceNow SDK (Now SDK) lets you build a scoped application as TypeScript source on your own machine, using Fluent — a declarative library where each platform artifact (table, business rule, script include, ACL, REST API, flow, ATF test) is a typed function call. You then run a build that transforms that code into deployable metadata and pushes it to an instance.

The point is engineering discipline: your app lives in Git, so you get real diffs, pull requests, code review, and repeatable CI/CD builds — instead of shuttling Update Sets between instances.

import { BusinessRule } from '@servicenow/sdk/core'
import { setOrderPriority } from '../server/set-order-priority'

BusinessRule({
    $id: Now.ID['set_order_priority'],
    name: 'Set Order Priority',
    active: true,
    table: 'x_myapp_order',
    when: 'before',
    action: ['insert', 'update'],
    script: setOrderPriority, // preferred: JS module (Now.include still works)
})

The declarative "when it runs" lives in the .now.ts file; server logic preferably lives in a src/server module with typed Glide APIs. A project has now.config.json (scope + scopeId), src/fluent, and now-sdk build / now-sdk install steps.

SDK vs App Engine Studio

  • Choose the SDK/Fluent for engineering-led teams that want Git, code review, TypeScript types, and CI/CD across environments.
  • Choose App Engine Studio / the platform UI for fast low-code work by admins and citizen developers, or small single-instance apps.
  • They coexist — an SDK-built app still opens in the platform.
Score points: mention that Now.ID['...'] maps to stable sys_ids in src/fluent/generated/keys.ts (never hand-edit; never invent sys_ids), that JS modules are preferred over inlined Now.include scripts, that now-sdk install pushes the build to an instance, and that ServiceNow/sdk-examples plus now-sdk explain are the canonical references.

question: What is ServiceNow, and why do enterprises use it? Explain it as if you're talking to someone who has never heard of the platform.
answer:
Why Interviewers Ask This

This is the most common opening question in any ServiceNow interview. Interviewers want to see if you understand the 'why' behind the platform — not just the technical definition, but the business problem it solves.

The Answer

ServiceNow is a cloud-based platform that helps organizations manage their digital workflows. Think of it as a single system where an entire company can track, automate, and manage work — from IT support tickets to HR onboarding to security incidents to customer service requests.

Before ServiceNow, most companies had dozens of disconnected tools: one for IT tickets, another for change management, another for HR requests, another for asset tracking. Each team had their own spreadsheet, email inbox, or legacy tool. Nothing talked to each other. When an employee needed a laptop, they'd email IT, who'd email procurement, who'd email finance — all manually, with no visibility into where the request stood.

ServiceNow replaces that chaos with a single platform where:

  • Everything is a record on a table — incidents, changes, requests, assets, users — all stored in one connected database.
  • Workflows automate the boring stuff — approvals route automatically, notifications fire on schedule, escalations happen without someone remembering to follow up.
  • Everyone sees the same data — the employee sees their request status, the manager sees their team's workload, leadership sees dashboards and trends.

Why Enterprises Pay Millions for It

  • Scale: ServiceNow handles tens of thousands of users and millions of records. Fortune 500 companies run their entire IT operations on it.
  • Single platform: Instead of 20 tools with 20 vendors and 20 integration headaches, one platform handles IT Service Management (ITSM), IT Operations (ITOM), HR Service Delivery, Security Operations (SecOps), Customer Service (CSM), and more.
  • Out-of-the-box processes: ServiceNow comes with ITIL-aligned processes pre-built. Companies don't start from scratch — they configure and extend what's already there.
💡 Interview Tip

Don't just say 'it's a ticketing tool.' That's the fastest way to lose points. ServiceNow is a platform — ticketing is just one use case. Show that you understand it's an enterprise workflow engine that spans IT, HR, Security, and Customer Service.

question: What is ITSM, and what are the core ITIL processes that ServiceNow supports out of the box?
answer:
What This Question Really Tests

Almost every ServiceNow role touches ITSM (IT Service Management). Interviewers ask this to verify you understand the foundational processes — not just the tool, but the framework behind it.

The Answer

ITSM is a set of practices for managing IT services to meet business needs. ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) is the most widely adopted framework that defines these practices. ServiceNow implements ITIL processes as ready-to-use modules.

The Core ITIL Processes in ServiceNow

  • Incident Management: Something is broken right now. A user can't log in, a server is down, email isn't working. Goal: restore normal service as fast as possible. ServiceNow table: incident.
  • Problem Management: WHY did it break? After the fire is out, investigate the root cause so it doesn't happen again. A problem can be linked to multiple incidents. Table: problem.
  • Change Management: We want to make a change to the environment — deploy new code, patch a server, upgrade a network switch. Changes go through an approval and risk assessment process before implementation. Table: change_request.
  • Service Request Management: An employee needs something — a new laptop, software access, a VPN account. These are standard, pre-approved requests fulfilled through the Service Catalog. Table: sc_request / sc_req_item.
  • Knowledge Management: Documentation and self-service articles so users can solve common issues themselves. 'How do I reset my password?' → Knowledge Base article. Table: kb_knowledge.

How They Connect

// Real-world flow:
// 1. 50 users report 'email is slow' → 50 Incidents created
// 2. Service Desk links all 50 to one Problem → 'Exchange server memory leak'
// 3. Problem team identifies fix → Creates a Change Request
// 4. Change goes through CAB approval → Scheduled for Saturday night
// 5. Change implemented → Problem resolved → All 50 Incidents auto-closed
// 6. Knowledge article created: 'What to do if email is slow'
💡 Interview Tip

The classic follow-up is: 'What's the difference between an Incident and a Problem?' Incident = the symptom (something is broken NOW). Problem = the disease (WHY it keeps breaking). Nail this distinction and you'll stand out from 80% of candidates.

question: What are the different types of scripts in ServiceNow? List them, explain where each one runs, and give a one-line example of when you'd use each.
answer:
The Intent Behind This Question

This is a staple interview question because it tests whether you understand the client-server architecture. Many candidates mix up which scripts run where — and that's a red flag for interviewers.

Server-Side Scripts (run on the ServiceNow server)

  • Business Rules: Trigger automatically when a record is inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. Example: Auto-assign a P1 incident to the on-call team when it's created.
  • Script Includes: Reusable server-side JavaScript classes/functions. Called by Business Rules, other Script Includes, or from the client via GlideAjax. Example: A shared utility function that calculates SLA breach time, used by multiple Business Rules.
  • Scheduled Jobs (Scheduled Script Executions): Run on a defined schedule — daily, weekly, or at a specific time. Example: Every night at midnight, close all resolved incidents older than 7 days.
  • Fix Scripts: One-time scripts that run manually. Used for data cleanup or bulk updates. Example: Update all 5,000 legacy incidents to a new category structure after a migration.
  • Background Scripts: Ad-hoc scripts run by admins for testing or troubleshooting. Not saved or scheduled. Example: Quickly check how many open P1 incidents exist right now.

Client-Side Scripts (run in the user's browser)

  • Client Scripts: Trigger on form events — onLoad, onChange, onSubmit, onCellEdit. Example: When the 'Category' dropdown changes to 'Network', show the 'Network Device' field and make it mandatory.
  • UI Policies: Declarative (no-code) rules to make fields mandatory, read-only, or visible. Example: When Priority is 'Critical', make 'Assignment Group' mandatory — configured entirely through the UI, no code.
  • UI Actions: Custom buttons, links, or context menu items on forms or lists. Can run client-side, server-side, or both. Example: A 'Close and Notify' button that resolves the incident and sends the caller an email in one click.

The Golden Rule

// SERVER-SIDE: Has access to GlideRecord, can query/update database directly
// CLIENT-SIDE: Has access to g_form, g_user — manipulates the form in the browser
// 
// Client should NOT use GlideRecord (a legacy client-side GlideRecord exists, but it is
// unsupported in scoped apps and Service Portal). To get server data from client, use GlideAjax.
// This is the #1 mistake beginners make.
💡 Interview Tip

If the interviewer asks 'Can you use GlideRecord in a Client Script?' — the right answer is you shouldn't. A legacy client-side GlideRecord exists, but it makes a server round-trip per call, is not available in scoped apps or Service Portal, and is against best practice. The supported GlideRecord API runs on the server. The bridge between them is GlideAjax. Getting this right shows you understand the architecture.

question: Explain the difference between an Incident, a Problem, a Change Request, and a Service Request. Give a real-world scenario that connects all four.
answer:
Why This Comes Up in Interviews

This question tests your ITIL fundamentals. Every ServiceNow admin and developer needs to know these four record types cold — they're the backbone of ITSM.

The Four Pillars

  • Incident: Something is broken or not working as expected RIGHT NOW. Focus: restore service as quickly as possible. Not about finding root cause — just get things working again. 'The printer on floor 3 isn't printing.'
  • Problem: The investigation into WHY incidents keep happening. Focus: find the root cause and eliminate it permanently. 'Floor 3 printer fails every Monday because the print spooler service crashes during the weekly backup.'
  • Change Request: A planned modification to the IT environment that goes through approval and risk assessment. Focus: minimize disruption while implementing necessary changes. 'Schedule a maintenance window to move the print spooler to a separate server so the backup doesn't crash it.'
  • Service Request: A standard, pre-approved request for something the user needs. No break/fix, no investigation, no risk assessment — just fulfillment. 'I need a new toner cartridge for the floor 3 printer.'

A Scenario That Connects All Four

// MONDAY 9:00 AM
// 15 employees report: 'I can't access the CRM application'
// → 15 Incidents created (INC0045001 through INC0045015)
// → Service Desk applies workaround: restart the app server
// → All 15 incidents resolved

// TUESDAY 9:00 AM
// Same thing happens again! 12 new incidents.
// → Service Desk creates a Problem (PRB0002001)
//   'CRM application crashes every morning around 9 AM'
// → Problem team investigates: the database connection pool
//   exhausts at peak login time because the pool size is too small

// WEDNESDAY
// → Problem team creates a Change Request (CHG0003001)
//   'Increase CRM database connection pool from 50 to 200'
// → Change goes to Change Advisory Board (CAB) for approval
// → Approved for Thursday night maintenance window

// THURSDAY NIGHT
// → Change implemented, tested, closed successful
// → Problem resolved, linked to Change
// → All related Incidents auto-updated

// MEANWHILE (unrelated)
// → Employee submits a Service Request: 'I need CRM admin access'
//   (RITM0006001) — goes through standard approval workflow

Key Relationships

  • Multiple Incidents can be linked to one Problem
  • A Problem can generate a Change Request as its fix
  • A Change Request resolves the Problem, which closes the Incidents
  • Service Requests are independent — they're about fulfilling needs, not fixing issues
💡 Interview Tip

Memorize this: Incident = firefighting. Problem = detective work. Change = planned surgery. Service Request = shopping. That analogy alone will make your answer memorable.

question: What is a Business Rule in ServiceNow? Explain the different types (before, after, async, display) and when each one fires.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Business Rules are the most important server-side automation in ServiceNow. Every developer and admin needs to know the four types and their execution timing.

What Is a Business Rule?

A Business Rule is a server-side script that runs automatically when a record is displayed, inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. Think of it as an automatic trigger — you define WHEN it fires and WHAT it does.

The Four Types

  • Before Business Rule: Fires BEFORE the record is saved to the database. Use it to validate data, modify field values, or abort the save entirely.
    // Example: Auto-set priority based on impact and urgency
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  if (current.impact == 1 && current.urgency == 1) {
    current.priority = 1; // Critical
  }
})(current, previous);
  • After Business Rule: Fires AFTER the record is successfully saved. The database write is complete. Use it for things that depend on the record existing — sending notifications, creating related records, updating other tables.
    // Example: Create a task when a change request is approved
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  if (current.approval.changesTo('approved')) { // Use internal value; 'approved' is the value for the approval field
    var task = new GlideRecord('change_task');
    task.initialize();
    task.change_request = current.sys_id;
    task.short_description = 'Implement: ' + current.short_description;
    task.insert();
  }
})(current, previous);
  • Async (Asynchronous) Business Rule: Fires AFTER the save but runs in the background on a separate thread. The user doesn't wait for it to finish. Use it for heavy operations — external API calls, complex calculations, bulk updates.
    // Example: Sync incident data to an external monitoring system
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('MonitoringSystem', 'POST');
  rm.setStringParameterNoEscape('incident_id', current.number);
  rm.execute(); // Runs in background — user doesn't wait
})(current, previous);
  • Display Business Rule: Fires when a form is loaded (displayed) to the user. Does NOT run on list views, imports, or web service calls. Use it to calculate display-only values or pass data to client scripts via the g_scratchpad object.
    // Example: Show a warning message when a VIP's incident is opened
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  if (current.caller_id.vip == true) {
    g_scratchpad.isVIP = true; // Pass to client script
  }
})(current, previous);

Execution Order

// When a user clicks 'Save' on an incident form:
// 1. Client Script (onSubmit) — browser validates
// 2. Data sent to server
// 3. BEFORE Business Rules — server validates/modifies
// 4. DATABASE WRITE — record saved
// 5. AFTER Business Rules — post-save logic
// 6. ASYNC Business Rules — queued for background execution
//
// When a user OPENS a form:
// 1. Database read
// 2. DISPLAY Business Rules — prepare display data
// 3. Form renders in browser
// 4. Client Script (onLoad) — browser-side setup
💡 Interview Tip

The follow-up question is always: 'Can you access the previous object in an async Business Rule?' The answer is no — async BRs don't have access to the previous values because they run outside the original transaction. If you need to compare old vs new values, do it in a before/after BR and store the result.

question: What is a sys_id in ServiceNow? Why is it important, and where will you encounter it?
answer:
Reading Between the Lines

This seems like a basic question, but it reveals whether you understand ServiceNow's data model at a fundamental level. sys_id is everywhere in ServiceNow, and misunderstanding it causes real bugs.

The Answer

A sys_id is a 32-character globally unique identifier (GUID) automatically assigned to every record in every table in ServiceNow. It's the primary key — the one field that uniquely identifies a record across the entire instance.

// Example sys_id:
// 6816f79cc0a8016401c5a33be04be441
//
// Every record has one:
// Incident INC0010001 → sys_id: 5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005
// User 'John Smith'  → sys_id: 6816f79cc0a8016401c5a33be04be441
// Business Rule 'Set Priority' → sys_id: a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6

Why It Matters

  • Reference fields use sys_id: When an incident has a 'Caller' field pointing to John Smith, the database stores John's sys_id (not his name). The display name is resolved at render time.
  • APIs use sys_id: REST API calls reference records by sys_id. GET /api/now/table/incident/5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005
  • Scripts use sys_id: gr.get('5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005') fetches a specific record. gr.getValue('caller_id') returns a sys_id, not a name.
  • URLs contain sys_id: When you open an incident form, the URL includes sys_id=5137153cc611227c000bbd1bd8cd2005.

Common Mistakes

// MISTAKE 1: Comparing display value instead of sys_id
if (current.caller_id == 'John Smith')  // WRONG — comparing GlideElement to string
if (current.getValue('caller_id') == '6816f79cc0a8016401c5a33be04be441')  // CORRECT

// MISTAKE 2: Hardcoding sys_ids across instances
// sys_ids are PRESERVED during instance cloning.
// However, records created independently on separate instances
// (e.g., a Business Rule built by hand in dev and separately in prod)
// will have different sys_ids.
// Never hardcode sys_ids — use queries or system properties instead.

// CORRECT approach: Query by a stable identifier
var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
gr.addQuery('user_name', 'john.smith');  // Stable across instances
gr.query();
if (gr.next()) {
  var userId = gr.getUniqueValue(); // a string sys_id, safe to store and reuse
}
💡 Interview Tip

If asked 'What does getValue() return for a reference field?' — always say the sys_id. If you want the display name, use getDisplayValue(). This distinction comes up in almost every technical ServiceNow interview.

question: What is the difference between a Client Script and a UI Policy? When would you choose one over the other?
answer:
The Real Question

Both Client Scripts and UI Policies run on the client side (in the browser) and both manipulate the form. The confusion is real — interviewers want to hear you explain the clear boundary between declarative and scripted approaches.

UI Policy (No-Code / Declarative)

A UI Policy uses conditions configured through the UI to control field behavior — no code required.

  • What it can do: Make a field mandatory, make it read-only, show/hide a field.
  • How it works: You set a condition (e.g., 'Priority is Critical') and define actions (e.g., 'Set Assignment Group to Mandatory'). All configured via dropdowns — no JavaScript.
  • Best for: Simple, condition-based field behaviors that admins (non-developers) can manage.

Client Script (Code / Imperative)

A Client Script uses JavaScript to react to form events — much more flexible but requires coding knowledge.

  • Types: onLoad (form opens), onChange (field value changes), onSubmit (form is submitted), onCellEdit (list editing).
  • What it can do: Everything a UI Policy does, PLUS: show alerts, make API calls (GlideAjax), set field values dynamically, perform complex calculations, interact with multiple fields at once.
// UI Policy equivalent in Client Script:
// 'When Priority is Critical, make Assignment Group mandatory'
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
  if (isLoading) return;
  if (newValue == '1') { // Priority = Critical
    g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', true);
  } else {
    g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', false);
  }
}

Decision Guide

  • Need to make a field mandatory/read-only/visible based on a simple condition? → UI Policy
  • Need to set a field's value based on another field? → Client Script (onChange)
  • Need to call the server for data? → Client Script + GlideAjax
  • Need to validate before the form saves? → Client Script (onSubmit)
  • Need non-developers to maintain the rule? → UI Policy

Important Gotcha

If both a UI Policy and a Client Script control the same field, the UI Policy wins because it runs after the Client Script. This is a common source of bugs — one developer sets a field with a Client Script, another admin creates a UI Policy that overrides it, and neither understands why their change 'doesn't work.'

💡 Interview Tip

The safe answer is: 'Use UI Policy for simple field visibility/mandatory/read-only rules. Use Client Script for anything that requires logic, calculations, or server calls. And never use both on the same field — it creates conflicts.'

question: What are Update Sets in ServiceNow? How do you move customizations from a development instance to production?
answer:
Context

Every ServiceNow environment has separate instances (dev, test, prod). Update Sets are how you package and move your changes between them. This is the deployment mechanism — and understanding it is essential for any role.

What Is an Update Set?

An Update Set is a container that automatically captures every configuration change you make while it's active. When you modify a Business Rule, create a UI Policy, or add a field to a table — that change is recorded in your current Update Set.

The Migration Process

// Step-by-step deployment:
//
// 1. SET your Update Set (Dev instance)
//    System Settings → Developer tab → Select 'My Feature Update Set'
//    Everything you change is now captured here
//
// 2. MAKE your changes
//    Create Business Rules, modify forms, add fields, etc.
//    Each change = one record in the Update Set
//
// 3. COMPLETE the Update Set
//    Mark it as 'Complete' — no more changes can be added
//
// 4. EXPORT from Dev
//    Right-click → Export to XML (or use Remote instance connection)
//
// 5. IMPORT to Test/Prod
//    Retrieved Update Sets → Import from XML
//
// 6. PREVIEW
//    System previews all changes and flags conflicts
//    'This Business Rule already exists — overwrite?'
//
// 7. COMMIT
//    Apply all changes to the target instance

What Update Sets Capture (and Don't)

  • DO capture: Business Rules, Client Scripts, UI Policies, UI Actions, Script Includes, ACLs, form layouts, System Properties, Scheduled Jobs, Flow Designer flows, table schema changes (new fields/tables).
  • DON'T capture: Data records (incidents, users, CMDB CIs), homepage/dashboard configurations (user-specific), report definitions (sometimes), attachment content.

Common Mistakes

  • Wrong Update Set: Forgetting to switch your active Update Set before making changes. Your changes end up in the 'Default' Update Set and get mixed with other unrelated work. Always check your current Update Set before starting.
  • Missing dependencies: You create a Script Include in one Update Set and a Business Rule that calls it in another. If you deploy the Business Rule first, it fails because the Script Include doesn't exist yet. Always track dependencies and deploy in order.
  • Overwriting changes: Two developers modify the same Business Rule in different Update Sets. The second one committed overwrites the first — no merge, just overwrite. Communication is critical.
💡 Interview Tip

If asked 'How is this different from Git?' — explain that Update Sets capture configuration changes automatically (you don't 'commit' individual changes), there's no branching or merging, and the last commit wins on conflicts. For scoped applications, ServiceNow now offers Source Control Integration with Git, which is closer to what modern developers expect.

question: What is an ACL (Access Control List) in ServiceNow? How does it protect data?
answer:
Why This Matters in an Interview

Security is a core topic in every ServiceNow interview. ACLs control who can read, write, create, and delete data — and they're enforced automatically across the entire platform.

What Is an ACL?

An ACL is a security rule that controls access to tables, records, and individual fields. When a user tries to view an incident, update a change request, or delete a CI — the platform checks the ACLs to determine if that action is allowed.

The Three Components of an ACL

  • 1. Roles: Which role(s) does the user need? e.g., itil, admin, incident_manager. A user must have the specified role to pass this check.
  • 2. Conditions: Filter conditions on the record. e.g., 'Only if the record is assigned to the user's group.' This provides row-level security.
  • 3. Script: Advanced JavaScript logic for complex authorization. Returns true (allow) or false (deny).
// ACL Example:
// Table: incident
// Operation: write
// Role required: itil
// Condition: active=true
// Meaning: Users with 'itil' role can edit incidents, but only active ones

// ACL Script Example:
// Allow editing only if the incident belongs to the user's assignment group
answer = gs.getUser().isMemberOf(current.assignment_group);

Evaluation Order

  • ACLs are matched from most specific to least specific — the first match at each level is the one that gets evaluated:
  • incident.caller_id — field-level ACL (most specific)
  • incident.* — wildcard field ACL (covers any incident field without its own rule). The table/row-level rule is incident with field -- None --
  • *.* — global ACL (least specific)
  • To reach a field, the user must pass both the matching field-level ACL and the matching table-level ACL. But when several ACLs match at the same point (e.g., two ACLs on incident.caller_id), passing any one of them grants access (OR) — so adding another ACL at the same level can actually loosen access.

Key Facts for Interviews

  • Deny by default: If no ACL grants access, access is denied. Unlike some systems where everything is open unless restricted.
  • Admin overrides (not a blanket bypass): Users with the admin role always pass the role check, and pass the whole ACL when its Admin overrides box is checked (the default). When Admin overrides is unchecked, the ACL's condition and script still apply to admins.
  • Applies everywhere: ACLs enforce on UI, REST API, list views, reports, exports — not just forms.
💡 Interview Tip

The classic trick question: 'If I create a read ACL on the incident table requiring the itil role, and another read ACL on incident.priority requiring the incident_manager role — what happens when a user with only the itil role opens an incident?' Answer: They can see the incident (table ACL passes) but the priority field will be hidden/empty (field ACL fails). Both ACLs evaluate independently.

question: What is GlideRecord? Write a basic GlideRecord query to find all open P1 incidents assigned to a specific group.
answer:
Setting the Stage

GlideRecord is the single most important API in ServiceNow development. If there's one thing you need to know for any technical interview, it's this. Every developer, admin, and consultant uses GlideRecord daily.

What Is GlideRecord?

GlideRecord is a server-side JavaScript API that lets you query, insert, update, and delete records from any ServiceNow table. It's your primary tool for interacting with the database — like SQL queries, but in JavaScript.

Basic Operations

// === QUERY (SELECT) ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');     // Target the incident table
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);               // WHERE priority = 1
gr.addQuery('active', true);              // AND still open (excludes Resolved, Closed, Canceled)
gr.addQuery('assignment_group.name', 'Network Support'); // AND group name
gr.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');         // ORDER BY created descending
gr.setLimit(50);                          // LIMIT 50
gr.query();                               // Execute the query

while (gr.next()) {                       // Iterate through results
  gs.info('Incident: ' + gr.getValue('number'));
  gs.info('Caller: ' + gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id'));
  gs.info('Created: ' + gr.getValue('sys_created_on'));
}

// === INSERT ===
var newInc = new GlideRecord('incident');
newInc.initialize();
newInc.short_description = 'Server Down - Building A';
newInc.priority = 1;
// Look up the caller by user_name to get their sys_id
var caller = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
caller.addQuery('user_name', 'john.smith');
caller.query();
if (caller.next()) {
  newInc.caller_id = caller.sys_id;
}
var newSysId = newInc.insert();  // Returns the sys_id of new record

// === UPDATE ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');   // Get a specific incident
gr.state = 6;                     // Set state to Resolved
gr.close_notes = 'Fixed by restarting the service';
gr.update();                      // Save changes

// === DELETE ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');
gr.deleteRecord();                // Delete the record

Key Methods to Know

  • addQuery(field, value) — adds a WHERE condition
  • addQuery(field, operator, value) — adds a WHERE with operator (!=, >, <, IN, etc.)
  • addEncodedQuery(string) — adds a complex filter as encoded query string
  • query() — executes the query
  • next() — moves to the next record (returns false when done)
  • getValue(field) — returns the raw database value
  • getDisplayValue(field) — returns the display value
  • getRowCount() — executes a full COUNT(*) query; avoid on large tables. Use GlideAggregate with addAggregate('COUNT') instead
  • get(field, value) — shortcut to query a single record
💡 Interview Tip

When writing GlideRecord in an interview, always include setLimit() for queries on large tables, always use getValue() instead of dot-notation for field values, and never put GlideRecord in a Client Script — use GlideAjax for server data. These small details signal experience.

question: What is the Service Catalog in ServiceNow? How is it different from the regular incident form, and what happens when a user submits a catalog request?
answer:
Why Interviewers Ask This

The Service Catalog is one of the most visible parts of ServiceNow for end users. Interviewers want to see that you understand the full request lifecycle — not just the front-end form.

What Is the Service Catalog?

The Service Catalog is a self-service portal where employees can browse and request services or products — like an internal shopping site. Instead of sending emails or calling the help desk, users find what they need, fill out a form, and submit.

Catalog vs Incident — The Key Difference

  • Incident: Something is BROKEN. Reactive. 'My laptop won't turn on.' The goal is to fix it fast.
  • Service Request (Catalog): The user WANTS something. Proactive. 'I need a new laptop.' The goal is to fulfill the order through a defined process.

The Components

  • Catalog Item: A requestable service or product. 'Request a Laptop', 'VPN Access', 'New Hire Onboarding Package'.
  • Variables: The form fields specific to that item. Laptop model dropdown, justification text field, delivery date picker.
  • Variable Sets: Reusable groups of variables shared across multiple catalog items. A 'Delivery Address' variable set used by laptop, monitor, and phone requests.
  • Workflow / Flow: The backend process that handles approval and fulfillment.
